interactive.title: The Bystander Effect and Diffusion of Responsibility
interactive.text:
Social psychologists have recognized that other people’s presence influences our behavior, whether we are aware of it or not. One example is the bystander effect, a situation in which people are less likely to interfere during an emergency or when a social norm is being violated if there are others around. They feel less responsible because of the presence of other bystanders. This is known as diffusion of responsibility.

Most of the time people report that they don’t want to get involved and that’s why they don’t respond when they see something wrong. They assume someone else will step up and help. Researchers have found that people are less likely to help if they don’t know the victim.

Think about it this way, you’re walking to class and there are several students around. Someone falls on the ground having a seizure. What would you do? The bystander effect suggests that unless you know the person who has fallen, you are more likely to walk away than help. However, social psychologists believe that you are much more likely to help, or at least stop and check, if you are the only one around.

blanks.why: The subject “presence” is singular, so the verb is “influences”.
“Whether … or not” means “in either case”.
“One example is” introduces a case of the general idea.
“Less likely to do something” means less probable to do it.
“Others” is a pronoun meaning other people; “other” needs a noun after it.
“Is known as” gives the name of something; we say “is called diffusion…” without “as”.
“Get involved” means to take part in a situation.
“Someone else” means a different person.

distractors: Researchers have used scenarios such as this to understand social cognition in children.
Situationism is the view that our behavior and actions are determined by our immediate environment and surroundings.
Children with a negative bias, or hostile attributional error, are more likely to interpret the friend’s behavior as an aggressive or purposefully unkind act.
missing.why: It answers “What would you do?”, and the next sentence’s “However” contrasts with walking away instead of helping.

highlights.question: What makes people feel less responsible in an emergency?
When are you likely to help even a stranger, according to social psychologists?

idea.answer: People are less likely to help in an emergency when other people are present.
distractors: Children often see a friend’s unfriendly behavior as an aggressive act.
People are more likely to help a stranger than someone they know.
Our behavior is decided only by our personality, not by the situation.
idea.why: The passage explains the bystander effect: people step in less often when others are around.

titles.answer: The Bystander Effect and Diffusion of Responsibility
distractors: Interpreting and Responding to Social Situations
What Is Epilepsy and How Can You Help Someone With It?
titles.why: The whole passage explains the bystander effect and why people feel less responsible when others are present.

source.title: The Bystander Effect and Diffusion of Responsibility
source.note: “The Bystander Effect and Diffusion of Responsibility”, Introduction to Sociology 3e, OpenStax (Rice University), CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

interactive.title: Peopling Mesoamerica
interactive.text: To the south and west of the Eastern Woodlands, the climate is much more arid and less green. This desert scrubland extends down the center of Mexico to the tip of the Central Mexican Plateau. South of there, in the region often described as Mesoamerica, the environment is warmer, greener, and wetter. The formerly large-game-hunting peoples settled there after around 8000 BCE as the game disappeared and the bison followed the retreating grassland north. Evidence of Archaic peoples in this area has been found in several coastal sites along the Gulf of Mexico and the Pacific Ocean, as well as in the Tehuacán Valley south of modern Mexico City. They lived largely in small groups and hunted and gathered over large areas. During the dry season, they relied mostly on wild game like lizards, snakes, and insects, and edible plants like the agave. During the rainy season, they ate avocados, nuts, various types of fruit, and small game, like rabbits.

blanks.why: “Much” makes a comparative stronger: “much more arid”.
“Less” goes with adjectives (“less green”); “fewer” goes with plural nouns.
The singular subject “scrubland” needs the present-tense verb “extends”.
We say “described as”; “called” is used without “as”.
It matches the other comparatives, “greener, and wetter”, which contrast with the dry land to the north.
“Settled there” means settled in that place (Mesoamerica).
The peoples were only “formerly” big-game hunters because the large animals disappeared.
The bison moved north after the grassland, so they “followed” it (past tense).

distractors: Hunting bison was dangerous and required keeping a distance in order to not startle the animals or allow them to grow reflexively fearful of human presence.
In addition to bison, the plains peoples also hunted antelope, deer, and small animals like rabbits and birds.
In Mesoamerica it was squash and later maize, or corn, and in China millet and rice.
missing.why: It gives the foods of the dry season, which pairs with the next sentence about the rainy season.

highlights.question: What was happening to the large game and the bison when the hunters settled in Mesoamerica?
What did the Archaic peoples eat in the wet part of the year?

idea.answer: The Archaic peoples of Mesoamerica ate different foods in the dry season and the rainy season.
distractors: The Archaic peoples of Mesoamerica lived in large cities and grew maize.
Mesoamerica is drier and less green than the land to its north.
The bison adapted to the warmer climate and stayed in Mesoamerica.
idea.why: The passage lists lizards, snakes, insects and agave for the dry season, and avocados, nuts and fruit for the rainy season.

titles.why: The passage describes the land of Mesoamerica and the first peoples who settled and lived there.

source.title: Peopling Mesoamerica
source.note: “Peopling Mesoamerica”, World History, Volume 1, OpenStax (Rice University), CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

interactive.title: Speciation through Geographic Separation
interactive.text: A geographically continuous population has a gene pool that is relatively homogeneous. Gene flow, the movement of alleles across the range of the species, is relatively free because individuals can move and then mate with individuals in their new location. Thus, the frequency of an allele at one end of a distribution will be similar to the frequency of the allele at the other end. When populations become geographically discontinuous that free-flow of alleles is prevented. When that separation lasts for a period of time, the two populations are able to evolve along different trajectories. Thus, their allele frequencies at numerous genetic loci gradually become more and more different as new alleles independently arise by mutation in each population. Typically, environmental conditions, such as climate, resources, predators, and competitors, for the two populations will differ causing natural selection to favor divergent adaptations in each group. Different histories of genetic drift, enhanced because the populations are smaller than the parent population, will also lead to divergence.

blanks.why: A singular subject (“population”) takes “has”.
“Gene pool” is the fixed term for all the genes in a population.
After “the” we need a noun: gene flow is the movement of alleles.
Gene flow is easy (“free”) because individuals can move; an adjective follows “is relatively”.
“Their” is the possessive for “individuals”.
“Similar to” is the right pattern, and free gene flow keeps the two ends alike.
“At one end … at the other end” is a fixed pair.
When populations are separated, gene flow is stopped: “is prevented” (passive).

distractors: A mutation can change one allele into another, but the net effect is a change in frequency.
In population genetic terms, evolution is defined as a change in the frequency of an allele in a population.
Gorillas, for example, cannot successfully breed with Pan paniscus, the bonobo.
missing.why: “That separation” refers back to the populations becoming separated, and “the two populations” is what “their” refers to in the next sentence.

highlights.question: How does the passage define gene flow?
Which environmental conditions may differ for the two populations?

idea.answer: When two populations are separated for a long time, their genes slowly become more and more different.
distractors: Genetic drift has the strongest effect in very large populations.
Separated populations keep the same allele frequencies because new mutations stop appearing.
In a continuous population, an allele is usually far more common at one end of the range than at the other.
idea.why: The passage explains that separation stops gene flow, so the two populations evolve along different paths.

titles.why: The whole passage explains how geographic separation makes two populations grow genetically different.

source.title: Speciation through Geographic Separation
source.note: “Speciation through Geographic Separation”, Concepts of Biology, OpenStax (Rice University), CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

interactive.title: Industrial Society
interactive.text:
In the eighteenth century, Europe experienced a dramatic rise in technological invention, ushering in an era known as the Industrial Revolution. What made this period remarkable was the number of new inventions that influenced people’s daily lives. Within a generation, tasks that had until this point required months of labor became achievable in a matter of days. Before the Industrial Revolution, work was largely person- or animal-based, and relied on human workers or horses to power mills and drive pumps. In 1782, James Watt and Matthew Boulton created a steam engine that could do the work of twelve horses by itself.

Steam power began appearing everywhere. Instead of paying artisans to painstakingly spin wool and weave it into cloth, people turned to textile mills that produced fabric quickly at a better price and often with better quality. Rather than planting and harvesting fields by hand, farmers were able to purchase mechanical seeders and threshing machines that caused agricultural productivity to soar. Products such as paper and glass became available to the average person, and the quality and accessibility of education and health care soared. Gas lights allowed increased visibility in the dark, and towns and cities developed a nightlife.

blanks.why: “A rise in” something means an increase, and the Industrial Revolution came from more invention, not less.
“Made this period” needs an adjective, and so many inventions made it special.
Use “number” with countable nouns like “inventions”; “amount” is for uncountable nouns.
“Within a generation” means in less time than one generation.
Tasks that took months became possible in days, which shows a great speed-up.
“In a matter of days” is a fixed phrase meaning in only a few days.
The verb “rely” is always followed by “on”.
Before steam, people and horses powered the mills; the plural noun is needed after “or”.
“By itself” means alone, without help; “engine” is singular and not a person.

distractors: This could move a pump directly or work a crank to turn a wheel and work a machine.
It had also begun to enter a new phase of development.
By the late 1800s, the Industrial Revolution had spread beyond Great Britain.
missing.why: Like the sentence before it (“Instead of paying artisans…”), it shows work once done by hand being done by machines, this time on farms.

highlights.question: How much work could Watt and Boulton’s steam engine do on its own?
Which products could the average person now get?

idea.answer: New machines in the Industrial Revolution made many everyday tasks much faster.
distractors: The Industrial Revolution began in Great Britain and later spread to the United States.
Most people still paid artisans to spin wool and weave cloth by hand.
Machines made goods faster, but the goods were of lower quality than before.
idea.why: The passage says tasks that took months could be done in days, and it lists machines that changed daily life.

titles.why: The passage describes how new machines changed work and daily life as society became industrial.

source.title: Industrial Society
source.note: “Industrial Society”, Introduction to Sociology 3e, OpenStax (Rice University), CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

interactive.title: Fitness
interactive.text:
Not many exercise classes have a tea break in the middle. But Margaret Allen’s class has one. After a gentle warm-up and a few quick exercises, the 93-year-old great-grandmother lets her group sit down and relax with a cup of tea. Some of the eight people in the class look like they need a break, but Allen is not even sweating.

The general rule is that eating just before doing sport is not a good idea and especially not halfway through the class. But, on the afternoon I visit Allen’s class in Saltburn-by-the-Sea, they eat fruitcake during the break. The cake was made for Allen’s recent birthday by her 89-year-old sister, Joan.

The ladies have just finished their cake when Allen gets up again. She plays a lively Scottish song and there is lots of toe pointing and leg kicking. Forty-five minutes later, the class is finally over.

blanks.why: “Many” goes with plural countable nouns like “classes”.
A “tea break” is a short rest for a cup of tea; a “brake” stops a car.
“A few” is used with plural countable nouns like “exercises”.
“Let someone do something” takes a base verb with no “to”.
After “lets her group sit down and” we need a base verb, like “sit”.
“Is not even sweating” is the present continuous, and it contrasts with the people who need a break.
We say “do sport”, and after “before” we use the -ing form.
“Halfway through” means in the middle of an activity.

distractors: But after six weeks they saw the results and were surprised.
He saw that short bursts of very hard exercise were as effective as hours of normal exercise.
Performances at school sports days in the weeks ahead may bear out the findings.
missing.why: “But” contrasts with the rule against eating, and “fruitcake” prepares for “The cake was made…” in the next sentence.

highlights.question: What drink does Allen’s group have during the break?
Who baked the fruitcake for Allen’s birthday?

idea.answer: At the age of 93, Margaret Allen still leads a lively exercise class.
distractors: Allen’s students are not allowed to eat anything during the class.
Short bursts of very hard exercise work as well as hours of normal exercise.
Allen gets tired quickly and needs the tea break more than her students.
idea.why: The writer describes the 93-year-old leading warm-ups, exercises and a lively dance without even sweating.

titles.why: The passage is about staying fit through an exercise class, even at 93.

source.title: Fitness
source.note: “Fitness” (elementary version), OneStopEnglish corpus (Vajjala & Lučić, 2018), CC BY-SA 4.0

interactive.title: Stem Cells in the Human Body
interactive.text:
Our bodies are made up of trillions of small units, known as cells. However, at the very early phase of development, we were embryos consisting of only a tiny clump of cells. Cells in an embryo are in a primitive state, and we call them embryonic stem cells. Embryonic stem cells can develop into three types of cells, called ectodermal stem cells, endodermal stem cells, and mesodermal stem cells. These three types of stem cells then go on to form 200 different types of cells. For example, stem cells form the cells of your skin, the red blood cells in your blood, and the cells that produce the color of your eyes. Altogether, stem cells form all the organs and tissues in the body, such as the bones, kidneys, liver, blood, and brain. After birth, embryonic stem cells are no longer present in the body.

However, even in the bodies of children, adults, and elderly people, we find several types of stem cells. These stem cells can form some, but not all, of the 200 different cell types.

blanks.why: 'Be made up of' is a fixed phrase that means 'consist of'.
After 'phase of' we need a noun, and an embryo is the first stage of a person's development.
'Consisting of' means 'made of'; 'containing' and 'including' are not followed by 'of'.
'Embryo' is a singular noun that starts with a vowel sound, so it takes 'an'.
'We call them X' means 'we give them the name X'; the other verbs cannot be used this way.
'Develop into' means 'grow and change until it becomes'.
'Three types' is plural and points back to the types just named, so it needs 'These'.
'Go on to' is followed by a base verb, and stem cells form (make) other cells.

distractors: Ongoing cell differentiation allows cells to become specialized to do different jobs.
The empty egg is then injected with DNA from another mature cell, such as a skin or blood cell.
This cell divides mitotically to produce a multicellular organism.
missing.why: It says embryonic stem cells disappear after birth, which the next sentence contrasts with 'However, even in the bodies of children, adults...'.

highlights.question: Which groups of people still have some types of stem cells in their bodies?
How many types of cells do the three types of stem cells go on to form?

idea.answer: Stem cells can turn into the many different kinds of cells that make up the body's organs and tissues.
distractors: Doctors can treat brain injuries by putting new stem cells into the patient's body.
Embryonic stem cells stay in the body for the whole of a person's life.
The stem cells found in adults can form every one of the 200 cell types.
idea.why: The passage says stem cells form about 200 types of cells and all the organs and tissues of the body.

titles.answer: Stem Cells in the Human Body
distractors: Making Neurons from Human Stem Cells
titles.why: The whole passage explains what stem cells are and how they form the cells of the body, from the embryo to old age.

source.title: The Use of Stem Cells for Treatment of Diseases
source.author: Franka Luk, Elke Eggenhofer, Marc H. Dahlke, and Martin J. Hoogduijn
source.note: “The Use of Stem Cells for Treatment of Diseases”, Franka Luk, Elke Eggenhofer, Marc H. Dahlke, and Martin J. Hoogduijn (kids.frontiersin.org), CC BY 4.0; via the CommonLit CLEAR corpus

interactive.title: Overclocking
interactive.text: Overclocking is the process of configuring a computer processor or other electronic circuit to run faster than it was designed to. Overclocking allows a computer to be faster and more responsive. Overclocked processors tend to use more electricity and make more heat than those running at their intended speed. It is often necessary to install a better heat sink to avoid overheating the processor. If a processor is overclocked too high, it can damage the processor or make the computer unstable. Increasing the voltage to the processor can allow it to be run at even higher speeds where it would otherwise be unstable, but this carries an especially high risk of damaging the processor. Overclocking is usually done in the computer's BIOS setup utility. Most brand-name computers such as Dell, HP, and others do not allow overclocking in the BIOS setup utility, but custom-built computers usually do. It is also possible to do the opposite, called underclocking, where the processor is run at a lower speed than intended. This may be done to extend battery life and reduce heat output. Underclocking will not usually damage a processor and may in fact make it last longer.

blanks.why: A comparative like 'faster' is followed by 'than'.
'Allow something to do' is correct; 'let' and 'make' are followed by a verb without 'to'.
After 'use more' we need a noun for the power a processor uses: electricity.
A possessive word is needed before 'intended speed'; 'their' refers to 'those' processors.
After 'to' we need a base verb, and a heat sink is used to avoid (stop) overheating.
'Too high' means 'more than is safe', which explains the damage in the rest of the sentence.
'Make something + adjective': a computer that does not work reliably is unstable.
'A high risk of damaging' is a common phrase for a strong chance of harm.

distractors: Usually, the contents of RAM are accessible faster than other types of information storage but are lost every time the computer is turned off.
Intel Core processors are based on Pentium M technology.
Software is any set of machine-readable instructions that directs a computer's processor to perform specific operations.
missing.why: It introduces the BIOS setup utility, which the next sentence refers back to when it says brand-name computers do not allow overclocking there.

highlights.question: Why might someone choose to run a processor at a lower speed?
What may need to be fitted to stop an overclocked processor from getting too hot?

idea.answer: Making a processor run faster than intended can speed up a computer, but it also creates more heat and risk.
distractors: Information in a computer's memory is lost every time the computer is turned off.
Most brand-name computers make overclocking easy to do in their setup utility.
Underclocking is risky because it often damages the processor.
idea.why: The passage says overclocking makes a computer faster and more responsive but uses more electricity, makes more heat and can damage the processor.

titles.why: Almost every sentence is about overclocking: what it is, its benefits and risks, where it is done, and its opposite.

source.title: Overclocking
source.author: simple wiki
source.note: “Overclocking”, simple wiki (simple.wikipedia.org), CC BY-SA 3.0 and GFDL; via the CommonLit CLEAR corpus

interactive.title: Computer program
interactive.text:
A computer program is a list of instructions that tell a computer what to do. Everything a computer does is done by using a computer program. A computer program is written in a programming language.

Some examples of computer programs:

A web browser like Mozilla Firefox and Apple Safari can be used to view web pages on the Internet.

An office suite can be used to write documents or spreadsheets.

Video games are computer programs.

A computer program is stored as a file on the computer's hard drive. When the user runs the program, the file is read by the computer, and the processor reads the data in the file as a list of instructions. Then the computer does what the program tells it to do.

A computer program is written by a programmer. It is very difficult to write in the ones and zeroes of machine code, which is what the computer can read, so computer programmers write in a programming language, such as BASIC, C, or Java. Once it is written, the programmer uses a compiler to turn it into a language that the computer can understand.

blanks.why: 'Tell someone what to do' is the usual pattern; 'say', 'speak' and 'talk' cannot take 'a computer' as an object here.
'What to do' means 'the things to do'.
'Is done' is the passive form: the things a computer does are done by a program.
We say something is written in a language.
'Can be used to' is followed by a base verb, and a browser is used to view (look at) web pages.
'Can be used to' needs a base verb, and an office suite is used to write documents.
The subject 'Video games' is plural, so it needs 'are'.
'Hard drive' is the fixed name for the part of a computer that stores files.

distractors: Each assembly language is specific to a particular computer architecture and sometimes to an operating system.
One gigahertz is one billion cycles per second.
Some types of emulators require newer computers that have the right system requirements.
missing.why: It continues from the program being stored as a file and gives the step that 'Then the computer does what the program tells it to do' follows.

highlights.question: Why do programmers usually not write programs in machine code?
Where is a computer program kept on a computer?

idea.answer: A program is a set of steps, written by a programmer, that a computer reads and carries out.
distractors: Programmers must write every program directly in the ones and zeroes of machine code.
The CPU controls the other parts of a computer, much like a brain controls a body.
Old computer games can run on new computers with the help of special programs.
idea.why: The passage defines a program as a list of instructions that tell a computer what to do and says that programmers write them.

titles.why: The whole passage explains what a computer program is, gives examples, and says how programs are stored, run and written.

source.title: Computer program
source.author: simple wiki
source.note: “Computer program”, simple wiki (simple.wikipedia.org), CC BY-SA 3.0 and GFDL; via the CommonLit CLEAR corpus

interactive.title: Introduction to The Elements
interactive.text:
The whole universe is built of matter. Right now, you are surrounded by it. The air we breathe is matter, and all the things you see around you are matter. The odors you smell are matter and the sounds you hear are caused by the movement of matter in your ears.

Matter is everything that takes up space and has weight. Scientists say that matter has volume and mass. Matter is made up of tiny building blocks called atoms. The purest type of atom is called an element. The elements are what give matter its different qualities.

Today we can see atoms by using a special instrument called an electron microscope. An electron microscope lets us see things that are millions of times smaller than the things we can see with a powerful optical microscope.

Most of the matter around us has more than one element in it. But some matter is made up of just one element. If you have ever held a diamond, for example, it is made of just one element, Carbon.

blanks.why: 'Be surrounded by' means 'have something all around you'.
After 'we' we need a verb: 'breathe' is the verb, and 'breath' is the noun.
The subject 'all the things' is plural, so it needs 'are'.
'Take up space' means 'fill space'; the subject 'everything' is singular, so it needs 'takes'.
'Say that...' reports what someone states; 'tell' needs a person after it.
'Called atoms' means 'named atoms'.
'Element' is a singular noun that starts with a vowel sound, so it takes 'an'.
A possessive word for 'matter' is needed before 'different qualities'; 'it's' means 'it is'.

distractors: The chemical elements are organized on the periodic table.
Helium, for example, is the second-most abundant element in the Sun.
Moving around this proton is a single electron.
missing.why: 'But some' contrasts with 'Most of the matter', and the next sentence gives a diamond 'for example' of matter made of one element.

highlights.question: What causes the sounds that we hear?
What do scientists say matter has?

idea.answer: Everything around us is made of atoms, and an element is the purest type of atom.
distractors: Only 92 of the known elements are found in nature.
Most of the matter around us is made of only one element.
Atoms are too small to be seen with any instrument, even today.
idea.why: The passage says matter is made of tiny building blocks called atoms, and the purest type of atom is called an element.

titles.why: The passage introduces matter, atoms and elements, and explains what an element is.

source.title: Introduction to The Elements
source.author: wikijunior
source.note: “Introduction to The Elements”, wikijunior (en.wikibooks.org), CC BY-SA 3.0; via the CommonLit CLEAR corpus

interactive.title: Metabolism
interactive.text:
Metabolism is the name given to the chemical reactions which keep us alive. It happens in the cells of living organisms.

Reactions catalyzed by enzymes allow organisms to grow, reproduce, maintain their structures, and respond to their environments. The word ‘metabolism' can also refer to digestion and the transport of substances into and between different cells.

Metabolism is usually divided into two categories. Catabolism breaks down organic matter and harvests energy by way of cellular respiration. Anabolism uses energy to construct molecules such as proteins and nucleic acids.

The chemical reactions of metabolism are organized into metabolic pathways, or cycles, like the Krebs cycle. One chemical is transformed through a series of steps into another chemical by a series of enzymes. The metabolic system of an organism decides which substances it finds nutritious and which poisonous. For example, some prokaryotes use hydrogen sulfide as a nutrient, yet this gas is poisonous to animals. The speed of metabolism, the metabolic rate, influences how much food an organism will need, and how it is able to get that food.

blanks.why: 'Keep someone alive' is a fixed phrase.
The plural subject 'Reactions' needs 'allow', and 'allow' is followed by 'to'.
A possessive word for 'organisms' is needed before 'structures'.
'Refer to' means 'be used for'; after 'can also' we need a base verb that goes with 'to'.
'Be divided into' means 'be split into' groups.
'Break down' means 'split into smaller parts', which is what catabolism does.
'By way of' is a fixed phrase meaning 'through' or 'by means of'.
'Such as' introduces examples.

distractors: They consume carbon dioxide and produce oxygen as a waste product.
With the exception of ions, small substances constantly pass through plasma membranes.
Active transport mechanisms, collectively called pumps or carrier proteins, work against electrochemical gradients.
missing.why: It gives an example of the sentence before it: one substance can be nutritious to some organisms and poisonous to others.

highlights.question: What does the speed of an organism's metabolism affect?
Which molecules does the passage give as examples of what anabolism builds?

idea.answer: Metabolism includes reactions that break substances down for energy and others that use energy to build molecules.
distractors: Plants produce most of the sugars that living things use for energy.
Hydrogen sulfide is a useful nutrient for animals as well as for some prokaryotes.
Catabolism uses energy to build large molecules such as proteins.
idea.why: The passage divides metabolism into catabolism, which breaks matter down and harvests energy, and anabolism, which uses energy to build molecules.

titles.why: The whole passage explains what metabolism is, its two categories, its pathways and its speed.

source.title: Metabolism
source.author: simple wiki
source.note: “Metabolism”, simple wiki (simple.wikipedia.org), CC BY-SA 3.0 and GFDL; via the CommonLit CLEAR corpus

interactive.title: Anansi and the Basket of Money
interactive.text:
Rabbit owned a big farm with lots of vegetables and fruit. Even though Rabbit shared generously with his friend, Anansi was unhappy and jealous.

So, Anansi thought of a clever plan to take over Rabbit's farm. Soon Rabbit was left poor and homeless. Anansi was the proud owner of all Rabbit's land, vegetables, and fruit.

Anansi went to the market to sell his fruit and vegetables. He made so much money that he filled a big basket with it! With some of the money, he bought maize for his family, and put it on top of the money in the basket.

Anansi happily headed home with his basket on his head, singing. He was thinking about all the things he was going to buy with his money.

On the way it started to drizzle. Soon the drizzle turned into a heavy downpour. Anansi the Spider left his basket on the side of the road to shelter under a tree. But from there he kept a close watch on his precious basket.

blanks.why: 'A farm with lots of vegetables' means a farm that has them.
'Even though' shows a surprising contrast: Rabbit was generous, but Anansi was still jealous.
'Think of a plan' means 'have the idea for a plan'; the story is in the past tense.
After losing his farm, Rabbit had no place to live, so he was homeless.
After 'the proud' we need a noun: the owner is the person who owns something.
After 'to' we need a base verb, and people go to the market to sell things.
'So much ... that' shows a result: he had so much money that it filled a basket.
The story is in the past tense, and he used the money to buy maize.

distractors: Then, Anansi felt a pull on one of his legs.
The other rabbits quickly finished their meal and fell asleep.
In the morning, the farmer brought in food for the rabbits.
missing.why: It continues 'it started to drizzle' and explains why Anansi then needed to shelter under a tree.

highlights.question: Why did Anansi leave his basket at the side of the road?
Where did Anansi put the maize after he bought it?

idea.answer: After taking over Rabbit's farm, Anansi made a lot of money selling its fruit and vegetables.
distractors: Anansi shared the money he made at the market with Rabbit.
Rabbit gave his farm to Anansi because he wanted to help his friend.
Anansi carried his basket under the tree so that it would stay dry.
idea.why: The story says Anansi took Rabbit's farm with a clever plan and then made so much money at the market that it filled a basket.

titles.answer: Anansi and the Basket of Money
titles.why: The story follows how Anansi got his basket of money from Rabbit's farm and then had to leave it by the road in the rain.

source.title: Anansi and Vulture
source.author: Ghanaian folktale
source.note: “Anansi and Vulture”, Ghanaian folktale (africanstorybook.org), CC BY 4.0; via the CommonLit CLEAR corpus

interactive.title: The tree wife
interactive.text:
Once upon a time, there lived a man who had plenty of everything – a large fertile farm, with cattle, sheep, and goats. But, as he grew old, he grew sad, because one thing was missing. He did not have a wife.

Standing under a tree one day, he had a brilliant idea. If he couldn't find a wife, perhaps he could make one?

So he set to work to shape a beautiful woman from a strong branch of the tree. When he had finished making the statue, he touched her eyes, and they opened. He blew gently on her, and she came alive.

She was truly the most beautiful woman he had ever seen. He knelt before her, and asked her to be his wife.

He gave her a colorful apron, beads, and a head ring, the sign of a married woman. And he built her a house with the mud and grass that used to lie at the foot of her trunk. "Only one thing I beg of you," he said to his wife. "Never tell anyone where you come from."

blanks.why: 'Once upon a time' is the fixed way many stories begin.
'Who' introduces information about a person and is the subject of 'had'.
'Grow old' means 'become old'; the story is in the past tense.
You stand under a tree, below its branches.
After 'couldn't' we need a base verb, and 'find a wife' fits the meaning.
After 'a strong' we need a singular noun, and a branch is the part of a tree he could shape.
The story is in the past tense, and he touched (put his hand on) her eyes.
'Come alive' means 'start to live'.

distractors: Then he thought about what the old woman had said.
He let the baby play with his chains.
In the bush, he saw something shining on a rock.
missing.why: Asking her to be his wife explains why he then gives her a head ring, 'the sign of a married woman'.

highlights.question: What did the man use to shape the woman?
What did the man ask his wife never to do?

idea.answer: A man who had no wife shaped a woman from a tree, brought her to life and married her.
distractors: The man found his wife working on a farm near the forest.
The woman told everyone in the village that she came from a tree.
The man built his wife a house out of wood from the tree.
idea.why: The story tells how the man made a woman from a branch, she came alive, and he made her his wife.

titles.why: The whole story is about the woman the man made from a tree and married.

source.title: The tree wife
source.author: Southern African Folktale
source.note: “The tree wife”, Southern African Folktale (africanstorybook.org), CC BY 4.0; via the CommonLit CLEAR corpus

interactive.title: Ten lost boys
interactive.text:
In this community people are not allowed to go to the forest on Wednesdays, because that is their rest day.

Many believed that anybody going to the forest on that day would meet with misfortune.

In this village lived ten young boys who did not like going to school.

The months of June and July are a season for snails. During this season, boys from the village normally go in search of snails.

One Wednesday afternoon, the ten boys went to the forest to search for snails. The next day was a Thursday and the market day.

After a few hours in the forest, they collected enough snails, which made them so happy.

They decided to count the snails each member had. The boys forgot that time was not on their side.

Finally, they set off for the village, happily laughing and chatting.

But they lost their way. They walked through the forest in the dark. They tried to find their way home but to no avail.

blanks.why: 'Be not allowed to do something' means it is not permitted.
A possessive word for the people is needed before 'rest day'.
After 'would' we need a base verb, and 'meet with misfortune' means 'have bad luck'.
'Who' introduces information about the boys and is the subject of 'did not like'.
June and July are two months, so the plural noun 'months' is needed.
'During' is followed by a noun for a period of time, such as 'this season'.
'Go in search of' means 'go looking for'.
The story is in the past tense, and the boys went (traveled) to the forest.

distractors: They were all silent and did not know what to do.
She walked and walked, and after some time, she came to the tall tree in which the rain bird lived.
The giant Elephant was never scared of any animal in the whole forest.
missing.why: It shows the boys lost track of time while counting snails, which explains 'Finally' and why they ended up in the dark.

highlights.question: According to the passage, what kind of day is Wednesday for this community?
What were the boys doing as they started back to the village?

idea.answer: The boys stayed in the forest too long and could not find their way home in the dark.
distractors: The boys went to the forest on a Thursday because it was market day.
The boys could not find any snails, so they went home sad.
A young girl went into the forest to feed the bird that brought the rain.
idea.why: The passage says the boys forgot about the time and then lost their way while walking through the forest in the dark.

titles.why: The story is about the ten boys who went into the forest to collect snails and lost their way.

source.title: Ten lost boys
source.author: Felix Kwame Senanu, Lois Nyarkoah Adu, Martha Agyeiwaa Twum and Nancy Mensah
source.note: “Ten lost boys”, Felix Kwame Senanu, Lois Nyarkoah Adu, Martha Agyeiwaa Twum and Nancy Mensah (africanstorybook.org), CC BY 4.0; via the CommonLit CLEAR corpus

interactive.title: A Conclusion and a Beginning
interactive.text:
If you are new to astronomy, you have probably reached the end of our brief tour in this chapter with mixed emotions. On the one hand, you may be fascinated by some of the new ideas you’ve read about and you may be eager to learn more. On the other hand, you may be feeling a bit overwhelmed by the number of topics we have covered, and the number of new words and ideas we have introduced. Learning astronomy is a little like learning a new language: at first it seems there are so many new expressions that you’ll never master them all, but with practice, you soon develop facility with them.

At this point you may also feel a bit small and insignificant, dwarfed by the cosmic scales of distance and time. But, there is another way to look at what you have learned from our first glimpses of the cosmos. Let us consider the history of the universe from the Big Bang to today and compress it, for easy reference, into a single year.

blanks.why: After 'have' we need a past participle, and 'reach the end' is the usual phrase ('arrive' needs 'at').
A possessive word is needed before 'brief tour'.
'Mixed emotions' means feeling good and bad at the same time.
'On the one hand ... on the other hand' is a fixed phrase for two sides of an idea.
A person is fascinated by something; 'fascinating' describes the thing itself.
'On the other hand' completes 'On the one hand' from the sentence before.
A person feels overwhelmed by too much; 'overwhelming' describes the thing that causes it.
A subject pronoun is needed before 'have covered'; the writers covered the topics.

distractors: The word astronomy comes from the Greek words astron which means star and nomos which means law.
Ancient people used the positions of the stars to navigate, and to find when was the best time to plant crops.
Since the 20th century there have been two main types of astronomy, observational and theoretical astronomy.
missing.why: It adds another feeling ('also feel ... small'), and the next sentence answers it with 'But, there is another way to look at' it.

highlights.question: What does the writer say learning astronomy is similar to?
What does the writer suggest doing with the history of the universe to make it easier to think about?

idea.answer: Learning astronomy may seem difficult at first, but it becomes easier with practice.
distractors: Most beginners find the new words in astronomy easy to remember right away.
Light from a distant star shows us the star as it was many years ago.
The first chapter of the book explains how the Sun and planets formed.
idea.why: The passage compares astronomy to a new language: at first there seem to be too many new expressions, but with practice you master them.

titles.why: The passage closes a first tour of astronomy (a conclusion) and opens a new way of looking at the universe (a beginning).

source.title: A Conclusion and a Beginning
source.note: “A Conclusion and a Beginning”, Astronomy 2e, OpenStax (Rice University), CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

interactive.title: Speciation
interactive.text:
Speciation is the rise of a new species in response to an environmental change or pressure. Allopatric speciation, mentioned previously, is the most common form of speciation event. During allopatric speciation, a species diverges when two populations become isolated from one another and continue to evolve. This isolation is created by geographic barriers such as mountains, rivers, or oceans. A good example of allopatric speciation is the different species of squirrel found on the two sides of the Grand Canyon. Descended from a common ancestor, the squirrels became reproductively isolated from one another by the Grand Canyon, eventually resulting in different species.

Sympatric speciation involves species that are descended from a common ancestor and remain in one location without a geographic barrier. A good example is the East African cichlid fish, which experience reproduction isolation due not to a physical barrier but to females’ selection of mates with certain coloration. The amount of light that reaches different levels and depths of the lake impacts how colors in the males appear to the females. The East African cichlid fish are also a good example of adaptive radiation.

blanks.why: 'In response to' is a fixed phrase meaning 'as a reaction to'.
'The most common' is the superlative form of 'common'.
'When' introduces the situation in which a species diverges.
After 'become' we need an adjective: populations become isolated (separated).
'Isolation' is a singular noun, and 'This' points back to the isolation just described.
'A good example of' introduces a case that shows the idea.
'Found on' is a past participle meaning 'that are found (live) on'.
'Descended from a common ancestor' means coming from the same earlier animal.

distractors: When that separation lasts for a period of time, the two populations are able to evolve along different trajectories.
Polyploidy is a condition in which a cell, or organism, has an extra set, or sets, of chromosomes.
Gorillas, for example, cannot successfully breed with Pan paniscus, the bonobo.
missing.why: It introduces sympatric speciation, and the next sentence gives 'a good example' of it: fish isolated without a physical barrier.

highlights.question: Which three geographic barriers does the passage name?
Why do the cichlid fish become reproductively isolated?

idea.answer: New species can form when populations are separated by geography or while they still live in the same place.
distractors: An extra set of chromosomes is the most common cause of new species.
Sympatric speciation is the most common way that new species form.
The squirrels on the two sides of the Grand Canyon still belong to the same species.
idea.why: The passage describes allopatric speciation, with a geographic barrier, and sympatric speciation, in one location without a barrier.

titles.why: The passage defines speciation and explains both of its forms, with and without geographic separation.

interactive.title: Arctic mapping
interactive.text:
Google has made maps of the world’s highest mountains, the ocean floor, the Amazon rainforest and even shown us a bit of North Korea. They want to make maps of the whole world, but they have mostly stayed away from the Arctic.

Now, however, Google is starting a very important update to hundreds of years of polar map making – and it hopes that the map will help give a better understanding of life on the permafrost for millions of web users. A small Google team has flown to Iqaluit, the largest town in the Canadian territory of Nunavut. They have taken their warmest winter clothes, many laptop computers and an 18kg telescopic camera that they can fix to their backpacks.

The team spent four days collecting the images and information that will give the isolated community on Baffin Island something that people across the world who live in cities now take for granted. An Inuit mapping expert helped the Google team and curious locals followed them around.

blanks.why: 'The world's highest mountains' uses the superlative to mean 'the tallest'.
'The ocean floor' is the usual phrase for the bottom of the sea.
An object pronoun is needed after 'shown': Google has shown us something.
'But' shows the contrast between wanting to map the whole world and staying away from the Arctic.
'Stay away from' means 'not go near'.
'However' shows a change from the past (staying away) to now.
'A better understanding' uses the comparative adjective before a noun.

distractors: Sea ice covers the central parts of the Arctic Ocean all year-round.
Google has begun testing the electric car at its headquarters in Mountain View, California.
The company is building about 100 prototypes for a two-year test.
missing.why: It introduces the team and the cold place they went to, so the next sentence can say what 'They' took: warm clothes, laptops and a camera.

highlights.question: Who assisted the Google team during their visit?
What does Google hope the map will help web users understand better?

idea.answer: Google sent a small team to the Arctic to collect images for a new map of the area.
distractors: Google has already finished detailed maps of every part of the Arctic.
Google is testing a car that drives itself near its offices in California.
Sea ice in the Arctic is melting because temperatures on Earth are rising.
idea.why: The passage says Google has mostly stayed away from the Arctic, but a team has now flown to Iqaluit to collect images and information.

distractors: The Polar Sea Ice Melts: What Happens to the Fish Under the Ice?
titles.why: The whole passage is about Google's project to map the Arctic town of Iqaluit.

interactive.title: Astrophysics
interactive.text:
Astrophysics is the study of how stars and planets work, and how we can learn about them. Astrophysicists use physics to explain what astronomers find and see.

Astrophysics is also the study of how the Universe started and how it is changing with time. This part of astrophysics is called cosmology. For a long time bodies in the sky seemed to be unchanging spheres moving in a circle. But on Earth growth and decay happened, and natural motion was in a straight line. Therefore, people thought the celestial region was made of a fundamentally different kind of matter from that found on Earth.

During the 16th and 17th century, natural philosophers such as Nicolaus Copernicus, Johannes Kepler, Galileo, Descartes, and Newton, began to maintain that the celestial and terrestrial regions were made of similar kinds of material and were subject to the same natural laws.

blanks.why: 'The study of' a subject is a set phrase; 'studied' is a verb and 'student' is a person.
After 'can' we need a base verb, and we 'learn about' the things we study.
Scientists use physics 'to explain' what they see; 'explanation' is a noun and cannot follow 'to'.
The subject 'it' (the Universe) is singular, so the verb is 'is changing'.
'Part' is a singular noun, so it needs the singular word 'This'.
'Is called' gives the name of something: this part is called cosmology.
Objects such as stars and planets are 'in the sky'; we do not say 'on' or 'at' the sky.
'Seemed to be' means 'looked as if they were', which describes how people saw the sky.

distractors: Galileo was the father of both modern experimental physics and telescopic astronomy.
The word astronomy comes from the Greek words astron which means star and nomos which means law.
Isaac Newton used Galileo's ideas to create his three laws of motion and his law of universal gravitation.
missing.why: It describes things on Earth ('But on Earth ...'), which the next sentence needs for 'Therefore ... from that found on Earth'.

highlights.question: Why do astrophysicists need physics?
Which thinkers began to argue that the sky and the Earth follow the same natural laws?

idea.answer: In the past, people believed that objects in the sky were made of different matter from things on Earth.
distractors: Galileo used a telescope to study the night sky and the planets.
Newton explained why the planets move in ellipses instead of circles.
Copernicus and Newton proved that the sky is made of a special matter not found on Earth.
idea.why: The passage says people thought the celestial region was made of a different kind of matter from that found on Earth.

titles.why: The passage explains what astrophysics studies and how ideas about the sky changed; astronomy, Copernicus and planetary laws are only parts of that story.

interactive.title: Meet the Creatures of the Sea
interactive.text:
Corals are both plants and animals. Thousands of little algae live inside corals, and give them energy to grow. They have hard outer skeletons and grow into many different shapes. Plankton is the main source of food for many sea creatures. They are a mix of algae, bacteria, tiny animals, and the eggs and larvae of larger animals that float about with the ocean currents. Feather stars may look like plants, but they're really animals. They use their feather-like ‘arms' to catch and eat bits of floating plankton.

Parrotfish have strong teeth that form a parrot-like beak, which they use to scrape algae off hard coral. Some species don't mind eating bits of coral as well, and they later poop out a fine sand that washes up on land to form beautiful white beaches. Clownfish and sea anemones live together and help each other. The clownfish help the anemones by cleaning their tentacles and luring other fish for the anemone to eat. The anemones, in turn, allow the clownfish to hide among their poisonous tentacles without stinging them.

blanks.why: 'Both ... and' joins two things: corals are plants and animals at the same time.
Living things need 'energy to grow'; a noun is needed after 'give them'.
Corals 'grow into many different shapes'; after 'many different' we need a plural noun.
'The main source of food' means where most of the food comes from.
'A mix of' means several things together, which matches the list that follows.
'That' starts a clause describing the animals that float with the currents.
'But' shows a contrast: feather stars look like plants, yet they are animals.
Animals 'catch and eat' their food; 'to' needs a base verb.

distractors: Most reefs grow best in warm, shallow, clear, sunny and agitated waters.
They are not strong enough to swim against ocean currents.
Creatures like tiny crabs, octopuses, worms, snails, starfish, and fishes exist there.
missing.why: It introduces clownfish and sea anemones, which the next sentence explains with 'The clownfish help the anemones'.

highlights.question: What do parrotfish use their beak-like teeth for?
In what way do clownfish help sea anemones?

idea.answer: Clownfish and sea anemones help each other in useful ways.
distractors: Most coral reefs grow best in warm, shallow and clear water.
Parrotfish catch plankton with their feather-like arms.
Plankton is made only of tiny plants that live on the sea floor.
idea.why: The passage says clownfish clean the anemones and bring them food, while the anemones give the clownfish a safe place to hide.

titles.answer: Meet the Creatures of the Sea
distractors: How Scientists Reveal The Secret Migrations of Fish
titles.why: The passage takes the reader under the sea to meet many creatures: corals, plankton, parrotfish and clownfish, not only one of them.

interactive.title: Nuclear power plant
interactive.text:
The conversion to electrical energy takes place indirectly, as in conventional thermal power stations. The fission in a nuclear reactor heats the reactor coolant. The coolant may be water or gas, or even liquid metal, depending on the type of reactor. The reactor coolant then goes to a steam generator and heats water to produce steam. The pressurized steam is then usually fed to a multi-stage steam turbine. After the steam turbine has expanded and partially condensed the steam, the remaining vapor is condensed in a condenser. The condenser is a heat exchanger which is connected to a secondary side such as a river or a cooling tower. The water is then pumped back into the steam generator and the cycle begins again. The water-steam cycle corresponds to the Rankine cycle.

The nuclear reactor is the heart of the station. In its central part, the reactor's core produces heat due to nuclear fission. With this heat, a coolant is heated as it is pumped through the reactor and thereby removes the energy from the reactor. Heat from nuclear fission is used to raise steam, which runs through turbines, which in turn power the electrical generators.

blanks.why: 'Take place' is a fixed phrase meaning 'happen'.
The subject 'The fission' is singular, so it takes 'heats'; fission makes the coolant hot.
'Water or gas, or even liquid metal' gives a choice, so 'or' is needed.
'Depending on' means that the coolant changes with the type of reactor.
'Then' shows the next step in the process; 'than' is only used in comparisons.
Water is heated 'to produce steam'; 'to' needs a base verb.
'The steam turbine' is singular, so the present perfect is 'has expanded'.
'The remaining vapor' is the steam that is left after the turbine.

distractors: Every atom has in its center a very small nucleus.
Steam engines can power many kinds of machines including vehicles and electric generators.
The wind turbine's blades are turned by the wind.
missing.why: It says the core produces heat, which the next sentence refers to with 'With this heat'.

highlights.question: What substances can be used as the reactor coolant?
What is the condenser linked to?

idea.answer: In a nuclear power plant, heat from fission makes steam that turns turbines to produce electricity.
distractors: Nuclear power plants turn fission straight into electricity without using any steam.
The water in the plant is thrown away after it passes through the turbine.
Nuclear power stations harm the environment less than plants that burn oil or coal.
idea.why: The last sentence says heat from fission raises steam, which runs the turbines that power the generators.

titles.why: The whole passage describes how a nuclear power plant turns heat from its reactor into electricity.

interactive.title: Habitat
interactive.text:
A habitat is an ecological or environmental area that is inhabited by a particular species of animal, plant, or other type of organism. The term typically refers to the zone in which the organism lives and where it can find food, shelter, protection and mates for reproduction. It is the natural environment in which an organism lives, or the physical environment that surrounds a species population.

A habitat is made up of physical factors such as soil, moisture, range of temperature, and light intensity as well as biotic factors such as the availability of food and the presence or absence of predators. Every organism has certain habitat needs for the conditions in which it will thrive, but some are tolerant of wide variations while others are very specific in their requirements. A habitat is not necessarily a geographical area, it can be the interior of a stem, a rotten log, a rock or a clump of moss, and for a parasitic organism it is the body of its host, part of the host's body such as the digestive tract, or a single cell within the host's body.

blanks.why: 'Is inhabited by' means 'is lived in by', which describes a habitat.
'In which' is used after a place (the zone) to say what happens there.
After 'can' we need a base verb, and animals 'find food and shelter' in their habitat.
'The natural environment' is the usual phrase; an adjective is needed before 'environment'.
'That' starts a clause describing the environment around the population.
'Made up of' means 'consisting of'.
'Such as' introduces examples (soil, moisture, temperature, light).
'The availability of food' means how much food can be found; a noun is needed after 'the'.

distractors: Grass is their usual food; it wears the teeth down, but horses' teeth continue to grow during life.
An example is the adaptation of horses' teeth to grinding grass.
Touch could indicate to a plant that insects are landing on its leaves and trying to eat them.
missing.why: It follows the list of physical and biotic factors by explaining that each organism needs certain conditions, some more strictly than others.

highlights.question: What can an organism get from its habitat?
Apart from a geographical area, which objects in nature, such as parts of plants, can be a habitat?

idea.answer: A habitat is the place where a living thing lives and finds what it needs to survive.
distractors: Living things slowly change over many generations to suit their habitat better.
Any organism can live in any habitat as long as there is enough food.
A habitat is made only of non-living things such as soil, rocks and light.
idea.why: The passage defines a habitat as the area where an organism lives and finds food, shelter, protection and mates.

titles.why: Every sentence explains what a habitat is and what it can include.

interactive.title: Be Wise with Money
interactive.text:
People work and earn money to take care of their needs as well as their wants. What is the difference between need and want? You need a bicycle to get to school and back if there are no good bus facilities in your town. You dream about a new cricket bat – this is a want, not a need. We need healthy food to stay alive. We want food that is not only healthy, but also tasty, rich, juicy, hot, and served in nice restaurants.

Families spend money depending on the needs of each person in the family. Basic food, education, housing, safety, and saving for the future are all needs. If there is enough money left after spending on the needs, families then think about spending on wants. Ask your mother if this is the reason why she did not let you buy something you wanted? Ask her what she did with the money instead.

blanks.why: People work to 'earn money'; after 'work and' we need a base verb that goes with 'money'.
'Take care of' is a fixed phrase meaning 'look after'.
'The difference between A and B' is the usual phrase.
'If' gives the condition: you need a bicycle when there are no good buses.
The sentence contrasts 'a want' with 'a need', and 'a' needs a singular noun.
An adjective is needed before 'food', and healthy food keeps us alive.
'Not only ... but also' is a fixed pair.
Food is 'served in restaurants'; the passive needs the past participle 'served'.

distractors: If someone has money that can be invested, that money is capital too.
The government said that it wants customers to know that tips are voluntary.
For example, lands, factories, shops, tools and machines are capital.
missing.why: It explains that families spend on wants only when money is left, which the next sentence calls 'the reason' your mother said no.

highlights.question: When do you need a bicycle to travel to school?
What things does the passage list as needs for a family?

idea.answer: Families pay for their needs first and think about wants only if money is left.
distractors: Families should save all their money instead of spending it on anything.
Children should spend their pocket money on whatever they want.
A new cricket bat is a need for every child who goes to school.
idea.why: The passage says families think about spending on wants only if there is enough money left after the needs.

titles.why: The passage teaches how to use money wisely by putting needs before wants.

source.author: Mala Kumar

interactive.title: How Do Aeroplanes Fly?
interactive.text:
Sarla learned that human beings can fly too, but not like birds. We can fly to any city in the world in an aeroplane, one of mankind's greatest inventions.

With the help of this great machine, we can also experience the joy of being airborne. Birds are aerial creatures that do not need an external machine to fly. Usually, a bird's wings are bigger than the rest of its body. The wings are very light, making it possible for birds to fly. Aeroplanes are huge and very heavy. Just like birds, aeroplanes have wings on both their sides which help them to fly. The wings of the plane are shaped just like those of birds - curved on the top and flat on the bottom which helps them to fly high up in the sky. Birds flap their wings to fly, but of course we have never seen an aeroplane flapping its wings! Birds flap their wings as they use the wind to push their body upwards.

blanks.why: We fly to a place, and 'any city in the world' needs a singular noun for a place.
'Aeroplane' starts with a vowel sound, so it needs 'an'.
'One of ... inventions' needs a plural noun, and an aeroplane is something people invented.
'With the help of' is a fixed phrase.
'The joy of being airborne' is the happy feeling of flying; a noun is needed after 'the'.
'That' starts a clause that describes the creatures.
'Bigger than' is the pattern for comparing two things.
Light wings 'make it possible' for birds to fly.

distractors: Flap, flap, flap, she would flap her wings but she couldn't lift off the ground.
Goose flew for one day, straight over the highest mountains in the world.
Bounthy sits and listens to the birds sing with joy.
missing.why: It introduces the wings of aeroplanes, which the next sentence describes as 'The wings of the plane'.

highlights.question: How do a bird's wings compare in size with its body?
What shape are an aeroplane's wings?

idea.answer: Aeroplane wings are shaped like birds' wings, but aeroplanes do not flap them.
distractors: Aeroplanes are lighter than birds, so they can fly higher.
Birds need an outside machine to help them fly long distances.
An aeroplane's wings are flat on the top and curved on the bottom.
idea.why: The passage says plane wings are shaped like birds' wings, but we never see an aeroplane flapping its wings.

titles.why: The passage compares birds and aeroplanes to explain how aeroplanes fly.

source.title: How Do Aeroplanes Fly?
source.author: Aditi Sarawagi
source.note: “How Do Aeroplanes Fly?”, Aditi Sarawagi (digitallibrary.io), CC BY 4.0; via the CommonLit CLEAR corpus

interactive.title: Why hyenas limp
interactive.text: The oldest hyena said, "Let the strongest hyena stand on the ground and then let the rest of us stand on each other's backs. We will climb on one another's backs until we reach the clouds." They agreed and started climbing up on one another's backs. Soon, there were no more hyenas left remaining on the ground except the strongest one. After the last hyena climbed up, the hyena on the ground thought that the others had started eating. He asked, "Why don't you give me some of the food you're eating?" However, the hyenas did not reach the clouds. They didn't find any food and so they had nothing to give to the strongest hyena standing on the ground. The strongest hyena became impatient and moved to the left side. All the others came falling down to the right side. As a result, even today all hyenas limp on their right side.

blanks.why: 'The rest of us' means all the others.
'Each other's' is a fixed phrase meaning 'one another's'.
'Until' shows when the climbing will stop: when they reach the clouds.
They said yes to the plan, so 'agreed' fits and matches the past tense 'started'.
'There were' is used with the plural noun 'hyenas' in the past.
'Except' means 'but not': only the strongest hyena stayed on the ground.
'The last hyena' is the final one to climb up.
'Thought' is the past of 'think'; 'taught' and 'bought' only look similar.

distractors: Hyena ran after Goat and soon caught up with him.
Hyena complained that he had been given more work.
Goat took advantage of this and ran, back towards his village.
missing.why: It says the other hyenas fell to the right, which is why, 'as a result', hyenas limp on their right side.

highlights.question: What did the hyena on the ground believe the others were doing?
What did the strongest hyena do when he lost patience?

idea.answer: The hyenas fell down because the hyena at the bottom became impatient and moved.
distractors: The hyenas reached the clouds and shared the food they found there.
The smallest hyena was chosen to stand at the bottom of the tower.
Hyenas limp on their left side because they fell to the left.
idea.why: The strongest hyena moved to the left, so all the others fell down to the right side.

distractors: Friendship between a donkey and a hyena
titles.why: The story explains why all hyenas limp on their right side.

interactive.title: The Steppes
interactive.text: The Eurasian Steppe is a vast stretch of grassland running from Eastern Europe over the top of central Asia and China into Mongolia. For much of human history, the area was home to traveling bands of nomadic pastoralists who grazed herds and collided with settled agricultural societies in Persia, Russia, and China. Geographers divide the Eurasian Steppe into two zones: One is in the west near Ukraine, Russia, and Kazakhstan, and the other is in the east, close to China and Mongolia. In both areas, the vastness of the land supported large herds of goat, cattle, and sheep. The prevalence of horses enabled powerful warriors of many cultures to rule from the saddle but also gave their people the freedom to roam, migrate, and resist absorption into a large unified state. While much of their history is still debated, these various tribes of the steppes provided the origins for a great number of Turkic, Iranian, Mongolic, Uralic, Tibeto-Burman, and multiethnic peoples today.

blanks.why: Grassland reaching from Europe to Mongolia is 'vast' (very large); an adjective is needed before 'stretch'.
'Running from ... into ...' describes how far the grassland stretches.
'For much of' is used with an uncountable noun like 'history'.
'Be home to' means 'be the place where someone lives'.
'Who' starts a clause about people (the pastoralists) and is the subject of 'grazed'.
Geographers 'divide' something 'into' parts; the plural subject needs 'divide'.
'One ... and the other' is used when there are two things.
'Close to' means 'near'.

distractors: Thus, the ruling lineages formed an aristocracy of sorts.
Each clan had a ruling lineage from which leaders were selected and that intermarried with other lineages to avoid in-breeding.
They spoke languages unrelated to Chinese, such as Turkic or Mongolic, but a few such as the Jie may have even spoken Indo-European tongues.
missing.why: 'In both areas' refers to the two zones described in the sentence before it.

highlights.question: Where does the Eurasian Steppe stretch?
Besides helping warriors rule, what did horses give the people of the steppes?

idea.answer: Horses allowed the steppe peoples to travel freely and stay outside large states.
distractors: A colder, drier climate forced the steppe peoples to give up farming.
The steppe peoples lived in fixed cities with written languages and regular taxes.
Historians now agree on every detail of the history of the steppe tribes.
idea.why: The passage says horses gave the people the freedom to roam, migrate and resist absorption into a large unified state.

distractors: The Inner Asian Steppe and Chinese Dynastic Struggles
East-West Interactions in the Early Middle Ages
titles.why: The passage describes the Eurasian Steppe as a whole: its land, its two zones and its peoples.

interactive.title: Endosymbiosis
interactive.text: The origin of eukaryotic cells was largely a mystery until a revolutionary hypothesis was comprehensively examined in the 1960s by Lynn Margulis. The endosymbiotic theory states that eukaryotes are a product of one prokaryotic cell engulfing another, one living within another, and evolving together over time until the separate cells were no longer recognizable as such. This once-revolutionary hypothesis had immediate persuasiveness and is now widely accepted, with work progressing on uncovering the steps involved in this evolutionary process as well as the key players. It has become clear that many nuclear eukaryotic genes and the molecular machinery responsible for replicating and expressing those genes appear closely related to the Archaea. On the other hand, the metabolic organelles and the genes responsible for many energy-harvesting processes had their origins in bacteria. Much remains to be clarified about how this relationship occurred; this continues to be an exciting field of discovery in biology. Several endosymbiotic events likely contributed to the origin of the eukaryotic cell.

blanks.why: Something nobody could explain was 'a mystery' until the new idea appeared.
The passive 'was examined by' names the person who did the examining.
A theory 'states that' something is true; the singular subject needs 'states'.
'A product of' means 'a result of'.
'Over time' means 'as time passes'.
'No longer' means 'not any more'.
The past-tense verb 'had' matches the singular subject and the past time of the 1960s.
'Widely accepted' means accepted by many people; an adverb is needed before 'accepted'.

distractors: Normally, the DNA forms a long string within the nucleus.
The somatic cells make up the structural components of a body, such as the tissues, muscles, and organs.
Animal cells, plant cells, fungal cells, and protist cells are classified as eukaryotic, whereas bacteria and archaea cells are classified as prokaryotic.
missing.why: 'On the other hand' contrasts the Archaea in the sentence before with bacteria, and 'this relationship' in the next sentence refers to both.

highlights.question: According to the endosymbiotic theory, how did eukaryotes come about?
What does the passage say appears closely related to the Archaea?

idea.answer: Eukaryotic cells probably began when one simple cell started living inside another.
distractors: Plastids such as chloroplasts are found in every kind of eukaryotic cell.
Scientists refused to accept Margulis's idea for many years.
All the genes of eukaryotic cells came from bacteria.
idea.why: The endosymbiotic theory says eukaryotes came from one prokaryotic cell engulfing another and the two evolving together.

titles.why: The passage explains endosymbiosis: the theory that eukaryotic cells came from one cell living inside another.

interactive.title: A Lightweight Device for Breathing Underwater
interactive.text:
As colourful fish were swimming past him off the Greek coast, Cathal Redmond was convinced he had taken some great photos with his first underwater camera. But, when he looked at the results on dry land, the images were brown and murky. Having taken the pictures while holding his breath underwater, he blamed the limited time he had to set up the shots. All he needed, the industrial designer thought, was a little more time to properly capture the fish in their natural environment.

He vowed to make the little extra time needed a reality and the result is his invention of the Express Dive – a refillable air storage device, held in the mouth, that lets users swim underwater for two minutes. It is aimed at bridging the gap between snorkelling, with its limited scope, and scuba diving, which gives divers the freedom to breathe underwater but at the cost of using cumbersome and expensive gear. The prototype of the invention – which is still in the initial stages of testing individual parts – looks like a cross between a scuba mouthpiece and a water bottle.

blanks.why: 'Swim past someone' means to go by them; 'passed' is a verb and cannot follow 'swimming'.
After 'had' we need the past participle, and we 'take' photos.
'Look at' is the phrase for directing your eyes; only 'looked' is followed by 'at' here.
The plural subject 'the images' needs 'were' in the past.
'While holding' means 'at the same time as holding'.
'Hold your breath' uses the noun 'breath'; 'breathe' is the verb.
He thought the short time caused the bad photos, so he 'blamed' it.
'Set up' means 'prepare'; after 'to' we need the base verb.

distractors: It takes videos of life deep inside the ocean.
When we run, we breathe in and out much faster.
But if you look even closer at life in the reef, you can find equally astounding creatures the size of your fingernail and even smaller.
missing.why: It says he needed 'a little more time', which the next sentence calls 'the little extra time needed'.

highlights.question: What was wrong with the photos when he looked at them on land?
What does the prototype of the Express Dive look like?

idea.answer: Redmond invented a small air device so that swimmers can stay underwater longer.
distractors: Redmond's first underwater photos were bright and clear.
The Express Dive is already finished and sold in shops.
Scuba diving equipment is cheap and easy to carry.
idea.why: The passage says he created the Express Dive, which lets users swim underwater for two minutes.

titles.answer: A Lightweight Device for Breathing Underwater
distractors: Treasure Reef: Revealing the Hidden Creatures of Coral Reefs
What Is the Best Way to Take Care of Buildings?
titles.why: The passage is about Redmond's small, light breathing device, which avoids the heavy gear of scuba diving.

interactive.title: Solar System
interactive.text:
The Solar System is the Sun and all the objects in orbit around it. The Sun is orbited by planets, asteroids, comets and other things.

The Sun is a star. It contains 99.9 percent of the Solar System's mass. This means that it has strong gravity. The other objects are pulled into orbit around the Sun. The sun is mostly made out of hydrogen and helium.

There are eight planets in the Solar System. From closest to farthest from the Sun, they are: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. The first four planets are called terrestrial planets. They are mostly made of rock and metal, and they are mostly solid. The last four planets are called gas giants. This is because they are large planets that are mostly made of gas. Even though they are made of gas, they have much more mass than the terrestrial planets.

blanks.why: 'All the objects in orbit' means all the things that move around the Sun; the other words are not things that can orbit.
After 'is' and before 'by', the passive needs the past participle 'orbited'.
'Other' goes before a plural noun ('other things'); 'another', 'each' and 'every' need a singular noun.
The singular subject 'It' needs the verb 'contains': the Sun holds 99.9 percent of the mass.
'This means that...' introduces the clause that explains the result.
An adjective is needed before the noun 'gravity', and 'strong gravity' is the usual collocation.
Objects 'orbit around' the Sun, as the first sentence already says ('in orbit around it').
'Is made out of' tells us what material something consists of.

distractors: The bright rings of Saturn are, by far, the easiest to see.
The largest of the moons are as big as small planets and just as interesting.
Both asteroids and comets are believed to be small chunks of material left over from the formation process of the solar system.
missing.why: It gives the last four planets the name 'gas giants', and the next sentence explains that name with 'This is because...'.

highlights.question: What are the terrestrial planets mostly made of?
Which two elements make up most of the Sun?

idea.answer: The Sun holds almost all of the Solar System's mass, so its gravity keeps the other objects in orbit.
distractors: Jupiter and Saturn are mostly made of hydrogen that has been squeezed into a liquid.
The gas giants have less mass than the terrestrial planets because gas is light.
Every planet in the Solar System has at least one moon going around it.
idea.why: The passage says the Sun contains 99.9 percent of the mass, which gives it strong gravity that pulls the other objects into orbit.

distractors: Smaller Members of the Solar System
titles.why: The passage describes the whole Solar System: the Sun and the eight planets that orbit it, not just one group of objects.
