interactive.title: What are the parts of the stomach?
interactive.text:
At the top of the stomach is a tube where food comes in from the esophagus. When you swallow, this tube opens so food can go in the stomach.

The stomach is made of muscle. These muscles help to break down food by mashing it into smaller pieces. The muscles also make waves pushing the food further down the digestive track. This is called peristalsis and happens from the esophagus all the way to the large intestine.

The stomach is lined with glands. These special cells make a liquid that is released into the stomach. This liquid is called gastric juice. The gastric juice has acid in it and helps break down or digest food.

The bottom part of the stomach is called the pyloric area. At the bottom of the stomach is another opening. This leads to the small intestine.

blanks.why: 'Where' introduces a place: the tube is the place where food comes in.
The tube must open so that food can go in, and the singular subject 'this tube' needs 'opens'.
The next sentence says 'These muscles', so the stomach is made of muscle.
The plural subject 'These muscles' needs 'help', and 'help to break down food' fits the meaning.
We mash or break something 'into' smaller pieces.
'This is called...' is used to give the name of a process.
'From ... to' shows where the process starts and ends: from the esophagus to the large intestine.
'All the way to' is a fixed phrase meaning the whole distance to a place.

distractors: It is widely used in industry, and it is also made by the stomach to help digest food.
In high concentrations, hydrochloric acid can make acidic mists.
Liquids are an in-between state of matter.
missing.why: 'These special cells' refers back to the glands, and the liquid they make is named in the next sentence: 'This liquid is called gastric juice.'

highlights.question: Where does the opening at the bottom of the stomach lead?
How do the stomach muscles break down food?

idea.answer: Glands in the stomach make an acid juice that helps to digest food.
distractors: Hydrochloric acid made by the stomach is also widely used in industry.
The stomach muscles push food back up into the esophagus.
The liver can grow back even when only a quarter of it is left.
idea.why: The third paragraph says the glands make gastric juice, which has acid in it and helps digest food.

titles.answer: What are the parts of the stomach?
titles.why: The passage goes through the parts of the stomach in order: the top opening, the muscles, the glands and the bottom part.

interactive.title: Plebs
interactive.text:
Childhood for plebeians was very different compared to their patrician counterparts since they were expected to enter the workforce at a much earlier age. Plebeians typically belonged to a lower socio-economic class than their patrician counterparts, and therefore did not have as many household servants. As a result, plebeian children were responsible for maintaining the household and caring for their aging parents.

Education was limited to what their parent would teach them, which consisted of only learning the very basics of writing, reading and mathematics. Wealthier Plebeians were able to send their children to schools or hire a private tutor.

Plebeians in ancient Rome lived in buildings called insula, apartment buildings that housed many families. These apartments usually lacked running water and heat. Not all plebeians lived in these run-down conditions, as some wealthier plebs were able to live in single-family homes, called a domus.

Plebeian men wore a tunic with a belt at the waist and women wore a long dress called a stola.

blanks.why: We 'enter the workforce' when we start working, and 'to' needs the base verb.
'Much' goes before a comparative adjective, so 'a much earlier age' is correct.
'Than' needs a comparative, and a lower class explains why they had fewer servants.
'Therefore' shows a result: because they were poorer, they did not have as many servants.
'As a result' is a fixed phrase that introduces a consequence.
'Caring for' means looking after, and it has the same -ing form as 'maintaining'.
'Was limited to' means their education included only what their parents taught them.
'Which' refers back to what their parents taught them.

distractors: Some families change to address immediate needs, such as when elderly parents can no longer live on their own independently.
Heavier clothing was worn in the winter, lighter clothing in the summer.
It is the smallest family structure and is often found in societies where geographic mobility is valued.
missing.why: 'These apartments' refers to the insula, and 'lacked running water and heat' explains the 'run-down conditions' in the next sentence.

highlights.question: What did plebeian parents teach their children?
What did plebeian women wear?

idea.answer: Many plebeian children had to work and look after their homes from an early age.
distractors: Plebeian children usually had household servants to help them at home.
All plebeians lived in single-family homes with running water and heat.
Plebeian clothing was made from wool or flax and changed with the seasons.
idea.why: The first paragraph says plebeian children started work early and looked after the household and their aging parents.

titles.why: Every part of the passage describes the life of the plebeians: their childhood, education, homes and clothes.

interactive.title: The Brain and Thinking Across Cultures
interactive.text: Not only is perception influenced by culture but also more complex thought processes, such as problem solving and making dynamic decisions. A static decision is whether I buy a KitKat or a Snickers bar in a grocery. Dynamic decisions are those that are made over time in a changing environment, for example, when you think about what profession you might want to choose later in your life. This decision might change depending on who you meet, who you talk to, what you read about certain jobs, what jobs your parents have, or what your friends want to become. Another example of dynamic decision-making is what a fire-fighting commander does. The fire-fighting commander has to make many decisions to fight wild fires depending on, for example, how big or small these fires are, their location near or far from cities, the weather and wind, which can make the fire burn faster or slower, the number of fire-fighting trucks and helicopters, and how fast they can go, and the amount of water they have to extinguish the fire.

blanks.why: The passive 'is ... influenced by culture' needs the past participle.
'Not only ... but also' is a fixed pair.
'Whether' introduces a choice between two options: a KitKat or a Snickers bar.
'Those that are made' uses 'that' to refer back to 'decisions'.
'Over time' is a fixed phrase meaning gradually, during a period.
'For example' introduces an example of a dynamic decision.
After 'want to' we need the base verb 'choose'.

distractors: Often, we will choose the most comfortable or familiar option, but then we may never know whether the novel thing or person was a better choice.
The more power people have, the more choices they may be presented with, and the more they can mold and shape the systems in which they live through their decisions.
Common heuristics are the familiarity heuristic, affect heuristic, and scarcity heuristic.
missing.why: It introduces the fire-fighting commander as another example, and the next sentence describes the commander's many decisions.

highlights.question: Which two snacks are used in the example of a static decision?
What can make a wildfire burn faster or slower?

idea.answer: Some decisions, like choosing a career, are made over time and can change as a person's situation changes.
distractors: Mental shortcuts help people make decisions more quickly by making problems simpler.
A static decision is one that changes depending on the people you meet.
Fire-fighting commanders usually make only one decision at the start of a fire.
idea.why: The passage says dynamic decisions, such as choosing a profession, are made over time in a changing environment and may change.

titles.answer: The Brain and Thinking Across Cultures
titles.why: The passage explains that culture affects complex thinking and uses static and dynamic decisions as examples.

interactive.title: A crying unknown baby
interactive.text: There was a boy who was named John. He lived with his grandparents in a village called Daveyton Village in Free State. John grew up. He took a walk around the village and he saw a crying baby. He rushed there called for help. The community of the village rushed to him and asked him what happened. John replied "I was taking a walk and I saw a crying baby." The community asked him again and they said "Do you know this child?" John replied "No I don't." Then the community leader took a baby to his home. The next day John was called to a community meeting of the unknown baby. John was asked to go to Faith the farmer and the settlers who lived nearby the river where the unknown baby was found. John agreed on that brilliant and clever idea.

blanks.why: 'Who' is used for a person (the boy).
A past-tense verb is needed after 'He', and 'lived with his grandparents' tells us where his home was.
'Take a walk' is a common collocation.
The past tense 'saw' matches 'took' earlier in the sentence.
'The community of the village' means the people who live there, who later hold a meeting.
'Asked him what happened' uses 'what' for the event they want to know about.
'Was taking' is the past continuous, and we 'take a walk'.

distractors: They tried to get the children to notice that the baby was crying but the children kept on playing.
A group of cranes flew above the playground and felt sorry for the crying baby.
She put down her sleeping baby and climbed the tree.
missing.why: The community asks John whether he knows the child, and the next sentence is his answer: 'No I don't.'

highlights.question: Who took the baby home?
Where did John live with his grandparents?

idea.answer: John found a baby he did not know and called the people of the village for help.
distractors: John's grandparents took the baby to their home.
Cranes flew down and carried the crying baby away.
John knew the baby because it belonged to Faith the farmer.
idea.why: John saw a crying baby, called for help, and told the community that he did not know the child.

interactive.title: Hare and Hyena Make a Deal
interactive.text: Hare used to sit all day doing nothing and when Hyena came home after work, Hare would always ask him for nuts from his farm. But Hyena didn't like this very much. Hyena believes in working hard and not getting things for free. So, one day Hyena thought to himself, "Its so hard to work all day by myself. Maybe Hare could help me and in return he can get some nuts that he has actually worked for." Hare agreed to his terms and they shook hands on it because he thought it was a good deal. They also agreed that more work could be done and they will also get enough food for their families. The two worked so good together. They would work and laugh together. Hare would dig and plant and Hyena would help and sing along as they went. Hyena was very happy because he was able to plant a lot more than before. Hare was a really hard worker and worked all day long with no rest. He would work fast and faster. But he felt like he was working too much and wanted a raise because what Hyena was paying too little.

blanks.why: 'Doing nothing' means being lazy, which fits 'sit all day'.
After 'would' we need the base verb, and you 'ask someone for' something.
After 'didn't' we need the base verb 'like'.
'For free' is a fixed phrase meaning without paying or working.
'Thought to himself' means he said it in his mind; the story is in the past.
'In return' is a fixed phrase meaning as payment for something.
We 'agree to' someone's terms, and the story uses the past tense.
'Because' gives the reason why Hare shook hands: he thought it was a good deal.

distractors: Hyena complained that he had been given more work.
Hyena thought about this problem for a long time.
He would light a fire and roast the seeds.
missing.why: It shows that Hare worked very hard, which leads to 'He would work fast and faster' and to Hare feeling he was working too much.

highlights.question: What did Hare ask Hyena for when Hyena came home from work?
Why was Hyena very happy?

idea.answer: Hyena asked Hare to work on his farm so that Hare could earn his nuts.
distractors: Hare took Hyena's maize from the field at harvest time without asking.
Hyena did all the hard work on the farm while Hare rested.
Hare and Hyena decided to plant maize and share the duties equally.
idea.why: Hyena thought Hare could help him and in return get nuts that he had worked for, and Hare agreed.

interactive.title: The Rain Bird
interactive.text: When they stopped looking after the bird, the rain stopped falling. The crops began to dry up and die, and the animals grew thin and weak. Still, nobody in the village went into the forest to feed the bird that brought the rain. Now they were all too busy trying to find money to buy food in the neighboring town. One scorching day, a young girl called Ketti decided to go into the forest after school. "At least it will be cool in there," she thought. She walked and walked, and after some time, she came to the tall tree in which the rain bird lived. Ketti stared up at the tree. Suddenly, she remembered how her granny had taken her into the forest to feed the bird when she was still a tiny child. Ketti opened her school bag and pulled out a piece of bread left over from her lunch. Carefully she laid the bread at the base of the tree. Then because she had no thumb piano, she sang an old song that she had known all her life

blanks.why: 'Look after' means take care of, and 'stopped' is followed by an -ing verb.
Without rain, crops 'dry up' (lose all their water), and 'began to' needs the base verb.
'Nobody' means no person, which matches 'they were all too busy' in the next sentence.
We go 'into' a forest when we enter it.
'Too busy' means so busy that they could not do anything else.
People need money to buy food, and 'to' needs the base verb.
'Decided to go' means she made a choice; the story is in the past.
On a scorching (very hot) day, the forest would at least be cool.

distractors: The old man sat under the shade of a tree on the walkway and opened his bag.
She went to the forest because she did not know where else to go.
At the top of the tree, Ayanda saw the beautiful sun.
missing.why: It introduces the piece of bread that she lays at the base of the tree in the next sentence.

highlights.question: What did Ketti give the bird to eat?
Why did the villagers no longer go into the forest to feed the bird?

idea.answer: After people stopped caring for the rain bird, the rain stopped and the crops dried up.
distractors: Ketti went into the forest with her granny to look for snails.
The villagers fed the rain bird every day, even when they were busy.
Ketti played her thumb piano for the bird under the tall tree.
idea.why: The first sentences say the rain stopped when people stopped looking after the bird, and then the crops dried up.

titles.why: The story is about the bird that brings the rain and the girl who goes to feed it again.

interactive.title: The smell thief
interactive.text: One old woman especially loved the smells that drifted out of the bakery window every morning. This was Ma Shange who slept on a bench in the park every night. A few weeks before, a kind person had given her the money to buy herself a cinnamon bun. She had taken the bun back to the park and ate it very slowly, licking her lips and sharing the last crumbs with the birds. After that, although the old woman didn't have enough money to buy breakfast, she longed for the delicious bun again. So, every morning she walked slowly past Mr Shabangu's bakery, sniffing the air and smiling blissfully at the mouth-watering smell. Ma Shange's new habit made the baker very angry. As each day went by, he grew angrier and angrier with her. Finally, one winter morning when he was in an especially bad mood, he stormed out of his bakery and grabbed the old woman by the arm. "How dare you steal my smells!" he shouted. "You're nothing but a smell thief!" He wiped his hands on an apron, then pulled it off and threw it back into the bakery.

blanks.why: A plural noun is needed after 'the', and smells drift out of a bakery window.
'Who' is used for a person, Ma Shange, and it is the subject of 'slept'.
'Had' needs the past participle 'given'.
'Herself' refers back to the old woman, who buys the bun for her own use.
'Had' needs the past participle, and you 'take' something back to a place.
An adverb is needed to describe how she ate; 'very slowly' shows she enjoyed every bite.
'Although' shows a contrast: she had no money, but she still wanted the bun; 'despite' cannot start a clause.
'Longed for' means wanted something very much; the story is in the past.

distractors: Elephant noticed that someone was stealing his bananas.
He asked himself what the old woman thought he would do with the root.
But Hare did not steal that day or that night.
missing.why: It says Ma Shange's habit made the baker angry, and the next sentence says he grew 'angrier and angrier'.

highlights.question: Where did Ma Shange sleep at night?
What did the baker call the old woman?

idea.answer: An old woman who could not afford breakfast enjoyed smelling the bakery every morning, and this made the baker angry.
distractors: The baker gave the old woman a free cinnamon bun every morning.
Ma Shange took buns from the bakery without paying for them.
The old woman ate the whole bun quickly and gave nothing to the birds.
idea.why: Ma Shange walked past the bakery every morning to sniff the smells, and this new habit made the baker very angry.

titles.why: The story is about an old woman who loves the bakery smells and is called a 'smell thief' by the angry baker.

interactive.title: Divergent Planetary Evolution
interactive.text:
Venus, Mars, and our own planet Earth form a remarkably diverse triad of worlds. Although all three orbit in roughly the same inner zone around the Sun and all apparently started with about the same chemical mix of silicates and metals, their evolutionary paths have diverged. As a result, Venus became hot and dry, Mars became cold and dry, and only Earth ended up with what we consider a hospitable climate.

We have discussed the runaway greenhouse effect on Venus and the runaway refrigerator effect on Mars, but we do not understand exactly what started these two planets down these separate evolutionary paths. Was Earth ever in danger of a similar fate? Or might it still be diverted onto one of these paths, perhaps due to stress on the atmosphere generated by human pollutants? One of the reasons for studying Venus and Mars is to seek insight into these questions.

blanks.why: An adverb is needed before the adjective 'diverse'.
'Although' shows the contrast between the planets' similar start and their different paths.
The plural subject 'all three' needs the plural verb 'orbit'.
Planets orbit 'around' the Sun.
'Their' is the possessive form for 'all three' planets.
'As a result' is a fixed phrase that introduces the consequence of the diverging paths.
An adjective is needed after 'became', and cold Mars is contrasted with hot Venus.
'Hospitable' means pleasant to live in, which is true only of Earth, unlike hot Venus and cold Mars.

distractors: One of the major challenges presented by Venus is to understand why the atmosphere and surface environment of this twin have diverged so sharply from those of our own planet.
As more and more of the atmosphere escaped into space, the temperature on the surface gradually fell.
The greenhouse effect works on Venus just as it does on Earth, but since Venus has so much more CO2—almost a million times more—the effect is much stronger.
missing.why: It asks whether Earth could have suffered the same fate, and the next sentence continues the question about Earth with 'Or might it still...'.

highlights.question: What material did all three planets apparently begin with?
What might push Earth onto the same path as Venus or Mars?

idea.answer: Although Venus, Mars and Earth began in similar ways, they developed into very different worlds.
distractors: Mars is a smaller planet, so its gases escaped into space more easily than Earth's.
Scientists fully understand what caused the different climates of Venus and Mars.
Venus is much closer to the Sun than Earth, which explains its high temperature.
idea.why: The passage says the three planets started with the same mix of materials but their evolutionary paths have diverged.

titles.why: The passage is about how Venus, Mars and Earth started alike but evolved along different paths, not about one planet alone.

interactive.title: Cultural Evolutionism
interactive.text: Some anthropologists are interested in the origins of human cultural forms and how these forms have changed over long periods of time. Just as Charles Darwin applied the notion of evolution to explain how biological species change over time, many 19th-century anthropologists used evolution to explain how cultures changed over time. This approach is called cultural evolutionism. Like Darwin, these anthropologists believed that simple forms evolved into more complex forms. Comparing different cultures of the world, they assigned the ones they considered more rudimentary to earlier evolutionary stages, while the ones they considered more complex were assigned to the more advanced stages. For example, British anthropologist Edward Tylor argued that human culture evolved from savagery through barbarism to civilization. He identified savagery with people who used gathering and hunting to meet their basic needs. The domestication of animals and plants was associated with barbarism. Civilization resulted from more advanced forms of farming, trade, and manufacturing as well as the development of the alphabet. Not surprisingly, British scholars identified their own culture as highly civilized.

blanks.why: People are 'interested in' something; 'interesting' describes the thing, and 'curious' takes 'about'.
Darwin 'applied' (used) the idea of evolution; the past tense matches 'used' later in the sentence.
'Many' is used with plural countable nouns such as 'anthropologists'.
'Is called' gives the name of the approach.
'Like Darwin' means in the same way as Darwin, which matches 'Just as Charles Darwin' before.
A past-tense verb is needed after the subject 'these anthropologists', followed by a 'that' clause.
The -ing form 'Comparing' starts a phrase that describes what the anthropologists were doing.
'While' joins two contrasting clauses; 'during' must be followed by a noun, not a clause.

distractors: One very prominent scheme was proposed by the British anthropologist Edward Tylor.
All humans need to satisfy the need for food, clothing, and shelter.
Although popular among certain social scientists, social Darwinism was not a term often used in anthropology.
missing.why: 'He' refers to Tylor, and the sentence explains the first stage, savagery, before the next sentence explains barbarism.

highlights.question: What did these anthropologists believe about how cultural forms develop?
According to Tylor, what developments led to civilization?

idea.answer: Many anthropologists in the 1800s borrowed Darwin's idea of evolution to explain how cultures change.
distractors: Functionalism tries to understand each culture by asking how it meets people's needs today.
Tylor believed that all cultures were equally complex and could not be ranked.
Early anthropologists collected their information mainly from books written by other people.
idea.why: The passage says 19th-century anthropologists used evolution, as Darwin did for species, to explain how cultures changed over time.

distractors: The Development of Ethnography and Ethnology
titles.why: The whole passage describes cultural evolutionism: the idea that cultures develop from simple to complex stages, as in Tylor's scheme.

interactive.title: Contextual Influences on Cognitive Development
interactive.text:
Both Piaget’s theory and the information processing perspective are fueled by a feedback loop between the individual’s maturing brain and the environmental inputs and supports for the brain’s further growth and development. An example is the U.S. school curricula across grade levels. The preschool curriculum takes advantage of the playful mindset of the preoperational child, while high school curricula leverage adolescents’ newfound abilities and appreciation for complex problem-solving, introducing abstract concepts. This back-and-forth interaction between the individual and the environment is an example of contexts that influence cognitive development in adolescents. These contexts include family and home environment, culture and language, and formal schooling. In cultures that don’t emphasize the development of scientific reasoning, Piaget’s stage of formal operations may not be reached, and the features associated with adolescent thought might not be readily observed.

Considering family dynamics and the home environment, the authoritative parenting style shows the most benefit for school performance and engagement if the development of formal operations is considered a goal of cognitive development. Authoritative parents set high expectations with high levels of warmth and nurturing.

blanks.why: 'Piaget's theory' is a set of ideas, parallel to 'the information processing perspective'.
'Between ... and' is used for a link that connects two things.
'An example is...' introduces a case that illustrates the idea; 'An' must be followed by a single noun with a vowel sound.
'Take advantage of' is a fixed phrase meaning make good use of.
'While' joins two contrasting clauses about preschool and high school.
An adjective is needed before 'concepts', and abstract ideas suit adolescents' new problem-solving abilities.
A noun is needed after 'back-and-forth', and 'interaction between' describes a two-way influence.
'That' begins a clause describing the contexts.

distractors: It posits that cognitive development is continuous, rather than consisting of discrete stages.
Also, unlike Piaget’s theory, information processing theory is not the work of one theorist.
Parents also tend to guide children differently than when the children were younger.
missing.why: 'These contexts' picks up the word 'contexts' from the sentence before, and the following sentences discuss culture and family, two of the contexts it lists.

highlights.question: What do authoritative parents combine with high expectations?
What does the preschool curriculum take advantage of?

idea.answer: A young person's surroundings, such as family, culture and school, affect how their thinking develops.
distractors: Children from low-income families always score higher on tests of thinking ability.
Information processing theory says that thinking develops in separate stages, not continuously.
Every adolescent reaches Piaget's stage of formal operations, whatever their culture.
idea.why: The passage says contexts such as family and home, culture and language, and schooling influence cognitive development in adolescents.

titles.why: The whole passage is about how surroundings such as school, culture and family influence cognitive development.

source.title: Contextual Influences on Cognitive Development
source.note: “Contextual Influences on Cognitive Development”, Lifespan Development, OpenStax (Rice University), CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

interactive.title: Bright Future
interactive.text:
On the top of a hill, above Northumberland’s beautiful Kielder Water lake, a group of people are waiting in a car park next to a strange wooden building. They are here because of the darkness and this is Kielder Observatory, the centre of Britain’s latest industry – astrotourism. The people who are waiting outside are lucky. Many more people apply for a night of stargazing at the observatory but not everyone can come because numbers are strictly limited.

Inside, the observatory’s founder and lead astronomer, Gary Fildes, speaks to his colleagues and volunteers. The team discusses that they might see the northern lights but Fildes doesn’t think they will. Instead, they decide to use their powerful telescopes to look at Jupiter and Venus and, later, to find stars such as Capella and Betelgeuse. An extra attraction is the appearance of the International Space Station.

Fildes is a leading figure in the UK’s growing astrotourism industry. The key moment for Northumberland came in 2013 when the entire national park, about 1,500 square kilometres in area, got Dark Sky Park status. It is the only one in England. Dark Sky Parks are rare.

blanks.why: You stand 'on the top of a hill' above a lake; 'a' needs a singular noun.
'Are waiting' is the present continuous, and the next sentences repeat 'waiting outside'.
'Because of' gives the reason; 'since', 'due', 'although' and 'despite' do not go with 'of' here.
'Who' is used for people and is the subject of 'are waiting'.
The plural subject 'people' needs 'apply', and you 'apply for' a place.
'Not everyone can come' means only some of the people can visit.
An adverb is needed before 'limited', and strict limits explain why not everyone can come.
The singular subject 'Gary Fildes' needs 'speaks', and the text is in the present tense.

distractors: It is the only planet known to have life on it.
The resolution of a visible-light or infrared telescope is degraded by turbulence in Earth’s atmosphere.
The pop-up park is a simple idea.
missing.why: It introduces Dark Sky Park status, and the next sentence says 'It is the only one in England'.

highlights.question: Which planets does the team decide to look at with their telescopes?
Why are some people who apply not able to visit the observatory?

idea.answer: Kielder Observatory attracts visitors who come to look at the stars in the dark night sky.
distractors: Anyone who wants to visit the observatory can come on any night.
Kielder is one of many Dark Sky Parks in England.
The best observatories are built where the weather is clear and the air is dry.
idea.why: The passage says people come to Kielder Observatory because of the darkness, to spend a night stargazing.

titles.why: The passage is about astrotourism, a growing new industry in Northumberland with a bright future; telescopes are only one detail.

source.title: Bright Future
source.note: “Bright Future” (elementary version), OneStopEnglish corpus (Vajjala & Lučić, 2018), CC BY-SA 4.0

interactive.title: Firewall (computing)
interactive.text:
In computing, a firewall is a network security system that monitors and controls incoming and outgoing network traffic based on predetermined security rules. A firewall typically establishes a barrier between a trusted internal network and untrusted external network, such as the Internet. Firewalls are often categorized as either network firewalls or host-based firewalls. Network firewalls filter traffic between two or more networks and run on network hardware. Host-based firewalls run on host computers and control network traffic in and out of those machines.

The term firewall originally referred to a wall intended to confine a fire within a line of adjacent buildings. Later uses refer to similar structures, such as the metal sheet separating the engine compartment of a vehicle or aircraft from the passenger compartment. The term was applied in the late 1980s to network technology that emerged when the Internet was fairly new in terms of its global use and connectivity. The predecessors to firewalls for network security were the routers used in the late 1980s, because they separated networks from one another, thus halting the spread of problems from one network to another.

blanks.why: 'That' starts a clause describing the system; 'who' is only for people.
'Incoming and outgoing' is a fixed pair for traffic that comes in and goes out.
'Between ... and ...' is used for a barrier separating two things.
'External' contrasts with 'internal' earlier in the sentence and describes the Internet.
'Either ... or' presents two choices; 'neither' needs 'nor' and 'both' needs 'and'.
Firewalls 'filter' traffic; the plural subject 'Network firewalls' needs 'filter', not 'filters'.
Parallel with 'run', the plural subject needs the base verb 'control' (to manage traffic).

distractors: The origins of the Internet date back to research commissioned by the United States federal government in the 1960s to build robust, fault-tolerant communication via computer networks.
Network cards enable a computer to exchange data with the network.
Some network cards do not use a cable to connect to the network, but an antenna.
missing.why: The next sentence says 'Later uses refer to similar structures', so the sentence before must describe the original structure: a wall that stops a fire.

highlights.question: What did the word "firewall" mean before it was used for computer networks?
Why did the routers of the late 1980s stop problems from spreading between networks?

idea.answer: A firewall controls the network traffic that comes in and goes out by following security rules.
distractors: A firewall connects a computer to a local network through a cable or an antenna.
Firewalls were first built by the US government in the 1960s to make networks stronger.
Host-based firewalls are faster and safer than firewalls that run on network hardware.
idea.why: The first sentence says a firewall monitors and controls incoming and outgoing traffic based on security rules; the other ideas are never stated.

titles.why: The whole passage explains what a firewall is, its types and where its name came from; routers, network cards and cloud computing are not the main topic.

source.author: wikipedia

interactive.title: Dinosaurs in the Dark
interactive.text:
When you think of dinosaurs and where they lived, what do you picture? Do you see hot, steamy swamps, thick jungles, or sunny plains? Dinosaurs lived in those places, yes. But did you know that some dinosaurs lived in the cold and the darkness near the North and South Poles?

This surprised scientists, too. Paleontologists used to believe that dinosaurs lived only in the warmest parts of the world. They thought that dinosaurs could only have lived in places where turtles, crocodiles, and snakes live today. Later, these dinosaur scientists began finding bones in surprising places.

One of those surprising fossil beds is a place called Dinosaur Cove, Australia. One hundred million years ago, Australia was connected to Antarctica. Both continents were located near the South Pole. Today, paleontologists dig dinosaur fossils out of the ground. They think about what those ancient bones must mean.

blanks.why: 'Where they lived' asks about places, and the next sentence lists places.
'Thick jungles' is a common collocation; 'thickly' is an adverb and cannot describe a noun.
'Those places' points back to the plural places just listed.
'The cold and the darkness' needs a noun that matches the cold, dark poles in the title.
'Used to believe' is a fixed form for something people believed in the past.
Scientists believed dinosaurs lived only in hot places, so 'the warmest parts' is right.
With 'today' and the plural subject, the present-tense verb 'live' is needed.

distractors: Paleontologists and archaeologists are scientists who dig up the ground to find fossils.
The North Pole is over an ice-covered ocean.
A fossil is any kind of life that is more than ten thousand years old and preserved in any form that we can study today.
missing.why: The next sentence talks about 'those surprising fossil beds', which only makes sense after 'bones in surprising places'.

highlights.question: In which parts of the world did paleontologists once believe dinosaurs lived?
Where were Australia and Antarctica one hundred million years ago?

idea.answer: Some dinosaurs lived in cold, dark places near the poles, which surprised scientists.
distractors: Summer at the South Pole is now colder than winter at the North Pole.
Dinosaurs lived only in hot swamps, thick jungles and sunny plains.
Paleontologists found many ammonite fossils while digging in the Himalayas.
idea.why: The passage says some dinosaurs lived in the cold and darkness near the poles and that this surprised scientists.

titles.why: The whole passage is about dinosaurs that lived in the cold and dark near the poles, which the title describes.

source.title: Dinosaurs in the Dark
source.author: Stephen Whitt
source.note: “Dinosaurs in the Dark”, Stephen Whitt (sites.ehe.osu.edu), CC BY-SA 3.0; via the CommonLit CLEAR corpus

interactive.title: How Sleep Changes as the Brain Grows
interactive.text:
As a newborn, you spent more time asleep than awake. But the older you get, the less you sleep. It is not just the amount of sleep that changes during development but, importantly, the balance between different sleep stages also changes. Generally, as you grow older, you get less and less slow-wave sleep, while the proportion of light non-REM sleep increases. Scientists believe that these changes in sleep may tell us about the brain's potential to reconstruct itself.

From infancy to adolescence, your brain undergoes major reorganization and optimization to deal with your daily needs and experiences. New connections between brain cells are built, connections you do not need are removed, and the communication of information along important neuron tracks speeds up. Crucially, when a specific part of the brain is under reconstruction, the neurons in that region show more slow rhythmic activity during slow-wave sleep.

blanks.why: 'Asleep than awake' compares two states; 'awake' is the opposite of 'asleep'.
'The older ..., the less ...' is a fixed comparative pattern; 'fewer' is only for countable nouns.
Sleep is uncountable, so we say 'the amount of sleep', not 'the number of sleep'.
'The balance between' different things is the natural phrase.
'As you grow older' needs the base verb after 'you' in the present tense.
'While' joins two clauses to show a contrast; 'during' and 'despite' cannot be followed by a full clause.

distractors: While awake, our brain wave activity is dominated by beta waves.
The frequency of a brain wave is how many brain waves occur in a second, and frequency is measured in Hertz.
Stage 1 sleep is a transitional phase that occurs between wakefulness and sleep, the period during which we drift off to sleep.
missing.why: 'These changes in sleep' refers back to the changes just described, and the idea of the brain reconstructing itself leads into the next paragraph about brain reorganization.

highlights.question: Which kind of sleep makes up a bigger share of our sleep as we get older?
What do neurons in a part of the brain that is being rebuilt show during deep sleep?

idea.answer: The way the brain is rebuilt while we grow up appears to be linked to slow-wave sleep.
distractors: Young children dream most clearly during REM sleep because their eyes move quickly.
The brain builds most of its new connections while a person is awake.
Older people need more sleep than newborns because their brains work harder.
idea.why: The passage says changes in sleep may show the brain's ability to rebuild itself, and that regions being rebuilt show more slow activity in slow-wave sleep.

titles.answer: How Sleep Changes as the Brain Grows
titles.why: The passage explains how sleep changes from birth to adolescence and how this is linked to the growing brain; it does not describe sleep stages, healthy habits or sleep talking.

source.title: From ZZZs to AAAs: Why Sleep Is an Important Part of Your Study Schedule
source.author: Emma James, Ann-Kathrin Joechner, Ann-Kathrin Joechner, & Beate E. Muehlroth
source.note: “From ZZZs to AAAs: Why Sleep Is an Important Part of Your Study Schedule”, Emma James, Ann-Kathrin Joechner, Ann-Kathrin Joechner, & Beate E. Muehlroth, CC BY 4.0; via the CommonLit CLEAR corpus

interactive.title: Seismology
interactive.text:
Seismology is the study of what is under the surface of the Earth by measuring vibrations on the Earth's surface. A person who does this is called a seismologist.

It is part of the science of geophysics, which studies the physics of the processes that formed the Earth and other planets.

Seismology is done by seismologists and geophysicists using devices to pick up the vibrations called geophones, hydrophones or seismometers.

Seismology can either be passive, just listening to vibrations caused by earthquakes and volcanic activity, or active, using small explosive charges to send vibrations into the ground.

Seismic detectors come in two types, one which measures up and down vibrations, and one which measures side to side vibrations. Both types use and arrangement of a magnet and a coil of wire which will convert the vibrations into an electrical signal which can be stored in a computer for analysis.

Seismologists can find the location of earthquakes by plotting received vibrations on a map. They can also pick up underground nuclear tests, and this is what many of the seismic recording stations were set up for.

blanks.why: After the preposition 'by' we need the -ing form 'measuring'.
'Who' is used for a person doing an action: 'A person who does this'.
'The Earth and other planets' – the Earth is a planet, so the other members must be planets.
In the passive 'is done by', 'by' introduces the people who do the action.
'Pick up' means to detect, which is what these devices do with vibrations.
'Vibrations caused by earthquakes' is a passive phrase, so the past participle 'caused' is needed.
'Either ... or' joins the two choices, passive or active.

distractors: Seismic data uses sound waves to create an image of the sediments beneath the ground.
P-waves may be transmitted through gases, liquids, or solids.
The seismicity or seismic activity of an area refers to the frequency, type and size of earthquakes experienced over a period of time.
missing.why: The next sentence begins 'Both types use ...', so the missing sentence must introduce two types of detectors.

highlights.question: How do seismologists work out where an earthquake happened?
What causes the vibrations that passive seismology listens to?

idea.answer: Seismologists learn what is under the Earth's surface by recording vibrations with special devices.
distractors: P-waves are the fastest seismic waves and reach a seismograph first.
Seismologists can predict exactly when the next earthquake will happen.
Seismic detectors do not need electricity, so they work far from any computer.
idea.why: The passage defines seismology as studying what is under the surface by measuring vibrations, using devices such as seismometers.

titles.why: The whole passage describes the science of seismology: what it studies, its tools and its uses, not one kind of wave or earthquakes alone.

source.title: Seismology
source.author: simple wiki
source.note: “Seismology”, simple wiki (simple.wikipedia.org), CC BY-SA 3.0 and GFDL; via the CommonLit CLEAR corpus

interactive.title: Ekai and the Domestic Animals
interactive.text: Ekai keeps all sorts of animals in his father's homestead. His mother Mrs. Anok has always supported Ekai in the purchasing of the animals. Goats, chicken, chicks, cattle, rabbits and a dog are Ekai's favorite animals. During holidays Ekai with the help of his sister will take the goats out to graze in the nearby river banks, have fun and make sure all their livestock are satisfied. At the grazing banks Ekai would hold one of the goats after it has taken water confirming how the goats are growing fat each and every day. Ekai has a dog pet called Bony. Every time Ekai is around he would give Bony food and a hot shower with a shampoo, that makes Bony a happy and healthy dog. In the morning Ekai and his sister will give the birds food and water before he takes breakfast. Besides him Bony the dog would play and let no other wild birds to disturb their birds.

blanks.why: 'All sorts of' is a fixed phrase meaning 'many kinds of'.
Animals are kept on a family's land and home, the 'homestead'; the other nouns are not places.
After 'has always' we need the past participle 'supported' (present perfect).
The subject is a list of several animals, so the plural verb 'are' is needed.
'With the help of' is the fixed phrase for getting help from someone.
After 'to' we need a base verb; goats are taken out to 'graze' (eat grass).
After 'are', the -ed adjective 'satisfied' describes how the animals feel after grazing.

distractors: So, Jackal jumped up and took the goats out to graze.
Bounthy sits and listens to the birds sing with joy.
Ekai's mother brought him new school uniform and a pair of black shoes with grey pair of socks.
missing.why: The last sentence talks about 'their birds' and 'him', so the sentence before must show Ekai caring for the birds.

highlights.question: How does Ekai keep his dog clean?
What does Ekai check when he holds one of the goats?

idea.answer: Ekai takes good care of his animals with help from his sister and his mother.
distractors: Ekai's father takes one bird to the forest every day to catch other birds.
Ekai sells his goats at the market during the holidays.
Bony the dog chases Ekai's birds away from the homestead.
idea.why: The passage shows Ekai feeding, grazing and washing his animals, with his sister helping and his mother supporting him.

titles.why: The whole story is about Ekai and the animals he keeps at home.

source.title: Ekai and the Domestic Animals
source.author: Mele Joab Silva Afonso
source.note: “Ekai and the Domestic Animals”, Mele Joab Silva Afonso (africanstorybook.org), CC BY 4.0; via the CommonLit CLEAR corpus

interactive.title: A father's lesson
interactive.text: Abula stole his mother's money to buy sweets. Even when she hid her money, he found it and took it. After eating all his sweets, Abula would play with his friends. After a while, Abula stopped going to school. He stayed out playing the whole day, only returning home in the evening. Abula's mother noticed this and became worried. "Our son is not behaving well. I do not think he is attending school. He is also stealing money from me," said Abula's mother. He said to his wife, "Next time, hide the money within the pages of a book. He never even opens a book, so the money will be safe there." The next day, Abula looked for his mother's money. He searched everywhere but he did not find anything. He decided to go to the nearest market to find some money.

blanks.why: After 'to' we need the base verb; you 'buy' sweets (you 'pay for' them).
'Even when' introduces a time clause: at the times she hid her money.
We 'play with' friends.
'Stop' is followed by the -ing form: 'stopped going to school'.
'The whole day' means all day long; 'hole' only sounds the same.
'Noticed this' refers to one situation – Abula staying away from school.
After 'became' we need an adjective; a mother whose son skips school becomes 'worried'.

distractors: But her mother could not afford the necklace.
The children were quiet and ate their food.
But with the gem's power, he won every single match he played with his friends.
missing.why: After Abula looks for the money, this sentence says he could not find it, which explains why he then goes to the market to find money.

highlights.question: Where did the father tell his wife to hide the money?
Where did Abula decide to go when he could not find any money at home?

idea.answer: Abula's father thought the money would be safe in a book because his son never read.
distractors: Abula's mother put all her money in a piggy bank under her bed.
Abula used the money he took to buy new books for school.
Abula's teacher told his mother that he had stopped coming to school.
idea.why: The father says Abula never even opens a book, so the money will be safe there.

titles.why: The story turns on the father's clever advice to hide the money in a book, a lesson about Abula not studying.

source.author: Abraham Bereket, Adonay Gebru
source.note: “A father's lesson”, Abraham Bereket, Adonay Gebru (africanstorybook.org), CC BY 4.0; via the CommonLit CLEAR corpus

interactive.title: First Day At School.
interactive.text: One day, as Kunle and his father were going to the market, his father thought, " Shouldn't I take Kunle to school? " As his father was thinking about going to school, he saw a school and asked Kunle if he would like to go to school. "Yes!" Kunle answered. Afterwards, Kunle and his father went to buy the school uniforms. After buying the school uniforms, Kunle and his father went back home to prepare his school materials for the next day. The next day he got prepared, ate his food and packed his bag. When Kunle got to school, he liked the teachings and he learnt things like: reading, sports, mathematics, science, civic education and verbal reasoning. At break time, Kunle played football with his new friends. As they continued playing ball, Kunle scored for the first time which made it 1- 0. After playing for some time, they rang the bell to go inside the class. After school ended, Kunle told his father all that had happened and his father was proud at his performance. Kunle also told his father that his teacher liked him and she was proud of him.

blanks.why: The subject 'Kunle and his father' is plural and the story is in the past, so 'were going' is right.
We say 'thinking about' something.
'Asked ... if' introduces a yes/no question in reported speech.
After 'would' we need the base verb: 'would like to go'.
After 'went to' we need a base verb, and the next sentence says 'After buying the school uniforms'.
After 'to' we need the base verb 'prepare'.
The story is in the past and the list 'got ..., ate ... and packed' uses past-tense verbs.

distractors: My friends were not able to score any goals.
We played until the field was full of sand.
The goal posts were made of two big stones.
missing.why: The next sentence says 'As they continued playing ball', so the sentence before must show Kunle starting to play with others.

highlights.question: Which subjects did Kunle learn on his first day at school?
How did Kunle's father feel about how Kunle did at school?

idea.answer: Kunle enjoyed his first day at school and made new friends there.
distractors: Kunle and his father saw friends playing football on their way to the market.
Kunle's team did not score any goals during break time.
Kunle's teacher was unhappy because he arrived late on his first day.
idea.why: The passage says Kunle liked the teachings and played football with his new friends.

titles.why: The whole story follows Kunle from deciding to go to school to telling his father about his first day there.

source.author: Peniel Ighedosa, Precious Ighedosa, Rob Owen

interactive.title: Hyena and Monkey
interactive.text:
The hyena and the monkey had an argument. They went to a judge to settle their differences.

After the judge listened to their case, he was afraid to pass judgement on their case.

He thought to himself, "If I condemn the hyena, it will eat all my cattle. And if I condemn the monkey, he will eat all my corn! So, what am I to do?"

The judge thought for a while, and said, "The case is too difficult for me to judge alone. You should go to the elders of the village."

So, the hyena and monkey went to the elders.

They told the elders about their disagreement.

After the elders listened to their case, they were also afraid to pass judgement.

If they supported the monkey, the hyena might eat their cattle. If they supported the hyena, the monkey might eat their corn. The elders told Hyena and Monkey that their case was very difficult.

blanks.why: They need a judge to settle their differences, so they had an 'argument' (a noun after 'an').
We 'go to' a person or place.
After 'to' we need the base verb; people 'settle' their differences to end an argument.
'Was afraid to' needs an adjective, and the judge's next words show his fear.
'Thought to himself' means he thought silently; the reflexive pronoun refers back to 'He'.
After 'will' we need the base verb, and a hyena would 'eat' cattle.
'What am I to do?' asks which action to take.

distractors: Hyena complained that he had been given more work.
Hare agreed to his terms and they shook hands on it because he thought it was a good deal.
Hyena suggested that it was good to plant maize.
missing.why: The next sentences explain the elders' fear ('If they supported the monkey ...'), so the missing sentence must say the elders were also afraid.

highlights.question: Where did the judge tell the hyena and the monkey to go?
What did the elders fear would happen if they supported the hyena?

idea.answer: Both the judge and the elders were afraid to decide the case because of what the animals might do.
distractors: The judge decided that the monkey was right and the hyena was wrong.
The hyena and the monkey agreed to share their cattle and corn.
Hyena and Hare were great friends who did many things together.
idea.why: The judge and then the elders were afraid to pass judgement because the hyena might eat their cattle or the monkey their corn.

titles.why: The whole story is about the argument between the hyena and the monkey and the people who are afraid to judge it.

source.title: Hyena and Monkey
source.author: Malualem Daba
source.note: “Hyena and Monkey”, Malualem Daba (africanstorybook.org), CC BY 4.0; via the CommonLit CLEAR corpus

interactive.title: Sponges
interactive.text:
Animals in subkingdom Parazoa represent the simplest animals and include the sponges, or phylum Porifera. All sponges are aquatic and the majority of species are marine. Sponges live in intimate contact with water, which plays a role in their feeding, gas exchange, and excretion. Much of the body structure of the sponge is dedicated to moving water through the body so it can filter out food, absorb dissolved oxygen, and eliminate wastes.

The body of the simplest sponges takes the shape of a cylinder with a large central cavity, the spongocoel. Water enters the spongocoel from numerous pores in the body wall. Water flows out through a large opening called the osculum. However, sponges exhibit a diversity of body forms, which vary in the size and branching of the spongocoel, the number of osculi, and where the cells that filter food from the water are located.

Sponges consist of an outer layer of flattened cells and an inner layer of cells called choanocytes separated by a jelly-like substance called mesohyl. The mesohyl contains embedded amoeboid cells that secrete tiny needles called spicules or protein fibers that help give the sponge its structural strength.

blanks.why: The plural subject 'Animals' needs 'include', parallel with 'represent'; sponges are part of this group.
'In contact with water' means touching water; the other words only look similar.
'Which' refers back to 'water'; 'who' is only for people.
'Body structure' is uncountable, so 'Much of' is needed, not 'Many of'.
Water moves 'through' the body (from one side to the other); the other words only look similar.
After 'can' the verbs are in the base form ('filter', 'absorb', 'eliminate'), and wastes are removed.
'Takes the shape of' is a fixed phrase meaning 'has the form of'.

distractors: Between these two layers is a non-living, jelly-like mesoglea.
The gut may be a simple sac or highly branched.
Gemmules survive hostile environments and can attach to a substrate and grow into a new sponge.
missing.why: The next sentence says water 'flows out' through the osculum, so the sentence before must explain how water first enters the spongocoel.

highlights.question: What separates the outer layer of cells from the inner layer of choanocytes?
What three things can a sponge do by moving water through its body?

idea.answer: A sponge's body is built mainly to move water through it so that it can feed and take in oxygen.
distractors: Sponges digest large pieces of food in a simple gut before passing it to their cells.
Most sponges live in fresh water, and only a few kinds live in the sea.
Sponges have a simple network of nerve cells spread across the body.
idea.why: The passage says much of the sponge's body is dedicated to moving water through it to filter food, absorb oxygen and remove wastes.

titles.why: The whole passage describes sponges: where they live, how water moves through them and how their bodies are built.

source.title: Sponges
source.note: “Sponges”, Concepts of Biology, OpenStax (Rice University), CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

interactive.title: Theoretical Perspectives on Culture
interactive.text:
Music, fashion, technology, and values—all are products of culture. But what do they mean? How do sociologists perceive and interpret culture based on these material and nonmaterial items? Let’s finish our analysis of culture by reviewing them in the context of three theoretical perspectives: functionalism, conflict theory, and symbolic interactionism.

Functionalists view society as a system in which all parts work—or function—together to create society as a whole. They often use the human body as an analogy. Looking at life in this way, societies need culture to exist. Cultural norms function to support the fluid operation of society, and cultural values guide people in making choices. Just as members of a society work together to fulfill a society’s needs, culture exists to meet its members’ social and personal needs.

Functionalists also study culture in terms of values. For example, education is highly valued in the U.S. The culture of education—including material culture such as classrooms, textbooks, libraries, educational technology, dormitories and non-material culture such as specific teaching approaches—demonstrates how much emphasis is placed on the value of educating a society’s members.

blanks.why: 'All' refers to several things here (music, fashion, technology and values), so the plural 'are' is needed.
'Based on' is a fixed phrase meaning 'using something as the starting point'.
'In the context of' means 'from the point of view of'; the other words only look similar.
'In which' refers back to 'a system'; 'who' and 'whom' are only for people.
'As a whole' is a fixed phrase meaning 'all together as one unit'.
A society with parts that work together is compared to the human 'body' and its organs.
'In this way' is a fixed phrase; 'way' is singular, so 'these' and 'those' do not fit.

distractors: Cultures evolve via new ideas and new ways of thinking.
Cultural change can happen through invention or discovery.
Symbolic interactionists examine stratification from a micro-level perspective.
missing.why: The next sentence begins 'For example, education is highly valued', which gives an example of functionalists studying culture through values.

highlights.question: According to functionalists, how do cultural values help people?
Which things are given as examples of the material culture of education?

idea.answer: Functionalists believe that culture exists to meet the needs of a society and its members.
distractors: Functionalists argue that culture mainly creates inequality between rich and poor groups.
Every society shares one main culture and has no smaller cultural groups.
Cultures change mainly through new inventions and discoveries.
idea.why: The passage says functionalists see culture as existing to meet its members' social and personal needs.

distractors: High, Low, Pop, Sub, Counter-culture and Cultural Change
titles.why: The passage introduces three theories for looking at culture and explains how one of them, functionalism, views culture.

source.title: Theoretical Perspectives on Culture
source.note: “Theoretical Perspectives on Culture”, Introduction to Sociology 3e, OpenStax (Rice University), CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

interactive.title: The Origins of Ancient Egypt
interactive.text:
Aside from the Nile, Egypt and the areas around it are today part of the expansive and very arid Sahara. But around 10,000 BCE, as the Neolithic Revolution was getting underway in parts of southwestern Asia, much of North Africa including Egypt was lush, wet, and dotted with lakes. The region was highly hospitable to the many Paleolithic peoples living there and surviving on its abundant resources.

However, beginning around 6000 BCE the grasslands and lakes began to give way to sand as the once green environment was transformed into the Sahara we recognize today. As the environment became more difficult for humans to survive in, they retreated to oases and rivers on the fringes. One of these areas was the Nile River valley, a long thin area of fertility running through the deserts of eastern North Africa and made possible by the regular flooding of the Nile. The Nile is the longest river in Africa, and the second-longest in the world after the Amazon. It originates deep in central Africa and flows thousands of miles north through Egypt before it spills into the Mediterranean Sea.

blanks.why: 'Aside from' is a fixed phrase meaning 'except for'.
'Part of' means 'one piece of'; 'apart' is a different word.
'North Africa' is one uncountable area, so 'much of' is needed, not 'many of'.
Land that is lush and dotted with lakes is 'wet', not dry.
'Peoples living there and surviving' uses two -ing forms joined by 'and'.
'However' shows the contrast between the green past and the later change to sand.
After 'was' we need the past participle 'transformed' (passive): the land was changed into desert.

distractors: Over thousands of years, these methods spread up the Nile River and across North Africa.
Here arose another civilization that was quite unique.
By approximately 1000 BCE, large populations in both north and sub-Saharan Africa supported themselves by working the land.
missing.why: The next sentence begins 'One of these areas was the Nile River valley', so the sentence before must mention areas such as oases and rivers.

highlights.question: What makes the Nile River valley fertile?
Into which sea does the Nile finally flow?

idea.answer: When North Africa turned into desert, people moved to places with water, such as the Nile valley.
distractors: Farming in Africa began along the Niger River before it spread to Egypt.
The Nile is the longest river in the world, longer even than the Amazon.
Around 10,000 BCE, Egypt was already as dry as the Sahara is today.
idea.why: The passage says that as the land became a desert, people retreated to oases and rivers, including the Nile River valley.

distractors: The Origins of the Indus Valley Civilization
titles.why: The passage explains how changes in the land drove people to the Nile valley, where Egyptian civilization later began.

source.title: The Origins of Ancient Egypt
source.note: “The Origins of Ancient Egypt”, World History, Volume 1, OpenStax (Rice University), CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

interactive.title: Still no flying cars
interactive.text:
We do not yet live in an age of flying cars, as predicted in the 1985 film Back to the Future II, but smartphones and other new technologies are creating exciting possibilities. Experts agree that economic and population changes, new technology, and environmental concerns are having a big effect on transportation.

With an ageing transport infrastructure, cities in the US have to change and improve their transportation. Experts and scientists now realize that old ways of reducing traffic congestion aren’t enough to solve the problems of population growth and carbon emissions, and transportation is now an environmental problem.

Big US cities like Los Angeles and Chicago are adding more bus lanes and pedestrian walkways, and expanding rail networks. At the same time, they are creating advanced technologies that will allow a vehicle to drive itself and communicate with other vehicles and its environment.

Here are three of the key ideas that experts predict will change transportation in the future.

blanks.why: 'Not yet' means 'not up to now'; flying cars still do not exist.
'As predicted in the film' is a short passive phrase meaning 'as the film said would happen'.
Things that cause excitement are 'exciting'; people feel 'excited'.
The plural subject 'Experts' needs the verb 'agree' before 'that'.
'Have an effect on' uses the noun 'effect'; 'affect' is a verb.
'Have to' means 'must'; the plural subject 'cities' needs 'have', and 'must' and 'should' are not followed by 'to'.
'Their' shows that the transportation belongs to the cities; 'there' and 'they're' only sound the same.

distractors: The tests will make sure all cars meet a limit of 80mg of nitrogen oxide per kilometre.
He says we need better research into systems for navigation.
The car does not have all the normal car controls, such as foot pedals.
missing.why: The next sentence says 'At the same time, they are creating advanced technologies', so the sentence before must say what big cities ('they') are already doing.

highlights.question: What are big US cities adding to improve how people travel?
What will new technology allow a vehicle to do?

idea.answer: Experts think that old ways of reducing traffic are no longer enough for US cities.
distractors: Flying cars, like the ones in Back to the Future II, are now common in US cities.
Europe will be the first place to make car makers use real-world emissions tests.
Using GPS on our phones is making people worse at finding their way.
idea.why: The passage says experts realize that old ways of reducing traffic congestion are not enough to solve the problems.

titles.why: The passage says flying cars have not arrived yet but explains how transportation in US cities is still changing.

source.title: Still no flying cars
source.note: “Still no flying cars” (elementary version), OneStopEnglish corpus (Vajjala & Lučić, 2018), CC BY-SA 4.0

interactive.title: Electrical cable
interactive.text: An electrical cable is made of two or more wires running side by side and bonded, twisted, or braided together to form a single assembly, the ends of which can be connected to two devices, enabling the transfer of electrical signals from one device to the other. Cables are used for a wide range of purposes, and each must be tailored for that purpose. Cables are used extensively in electronic devices for power and signal circuits. Long-distance communication takes place over undersea cables. Power cables are used for bulk transmission of alternating and direct current power, especially using high-voltage cable. Electrical cables are extensively used in building wiring for lighting, power and control circuits permanently installed in buildings. Since all the circuit conductors required can be installed in a cable at one time, installation labor is saved compared to certain other wiring methods.

blanks.why: The singular subject 'An electrical cable' needs 'is' in 'is made of'.
After 'two or more' a plural noun is needed, and a cable is made of wires.
'A single assembly' means one unit made from all the wires; 'lonely' and 'alone' describe people's feelings.
'The ends of which' refers back to the assembly, a thing, so 'which' is needed.
After 'can be' we need a past participle, and cable ends are 'connected to' devices.
'A wide range of' is a fixed phrase meaning many different kinds.
'That purpose' points back to the one purpose of each cable; 'those' and 'these' need a plural noun.
An adverb is needed after 'are used', and 'used extensively' means used a lot.

distractors: In a building this ground is carried to each electrical device on two wires.
The transformer is often part of the inverter and can't be seen.
If two computers send data at the same time, a collision will occur.
missing.why: The last sentence talks about installing conductors and saving installation labor, so the missing sentence must first introduce cables used for wiring inside buildings.

highlights.question: Where does communication over long distances take place?
What benefit comes from installing all the conductors in one cable at the same time?

idea.answer: Cables are made for many different uses, such as carrying power, sending signals and long-distance communication.
distractors: Ethernet has been the most common way to link computers in a network since the 1990s.
Copper is used to make cables because it is cheap and easy to stretch.
An electrical cable is usually made of a single wire that carries power to one device.
idea.why: The passage says cables are used for a wide range of purposes, including power and signal circuits and undersea communication.

titles.why: The whole passage explains what an electrical cable is and the many ways cables are used; Ethernet, voltage and copper are only related topics.

source.title: Electrical cable
source.author: wikipedia
source.note: “Electrical cable”, wikipedia (en.wikipedia.org), CC BY-SA 3.0; via the CommonLit CLEAR corpus

interactive.title: Lung
interactive.text: The lungs are the primary organs of respiration in humans and many other animals including a few fish and some snails. In mammals and most other vertebrates, two lungs are located near the backbone on either side of the heart. Their function in the respiratory system is to extract oxygen from the atmosphere and transfer it into the bloodstream, and to release carbon dioxide from the bloodstream into the atmosphere, in a process of gas exchange. Respiration is driven by different muscular systems in different species. Mammals, reptiles and birds use their musculoskeletal systems to support and foster breathing. In early tetrapods, air was driven into the lungs by the pharyngeal muscles via buccal pumping, a mechanism still seen in amphibians. In humans, the primary muscle that drives breathing is the diaphragm. The lungs also provide airflow that makes vocal sounds including human speech possible.

blanks.why: 'Including' introduces examples of the animals that have lungs.
'Are located near' means 'are found near'; it tells where the lungs are.
'On either side' means on each of the two sides; 'both' would need the plural 'sides'.
'Their function ... is to' tells what the lungs do; the plural 'functions' does not agree with 'is'.
After 'is to' a base verb is needed; the lungs extract (take) oxygen from the air.
'It' is the object of 'transfer' and refers to oxygen, which is singular.
Parallel with 'to extract', 'to release' needs a base verb; the lungs let carbon dioxide out.
'Gas exchange' names the process of taking in one gas and giving out another.

distractors: Vertebrates can be further divided into mammals, fish, birds, reptiles, and amphibians.
Asexual reproduction, except for occasional identical twinning, is absent in birds and mammals.
The number of vertebrates has declined by 52% over the last forty years.
missing.why: The sentences before describe the muscles that drive breathing in different animals, so the missing sentence names the main breathing muscle in humans.

highlights.question: Where are the two lungs found in mammals and most other vertebrates?
How was air moved into the lungs of early tetrapods?

idea.answer: The lungs take oxygen from the air into the blood and send carbon dioxide out of the body.
distractors: Fish and snails cannot breathe air because none of them have lungs.
Only mammals use muscles to move air into and out of their lungs.
Particles from car fumes and smoking can enter the lungs and cause damage.
idea.why: The third sentence says the lungs extract oxygen into the bloodstream and release carbon dioxide into the atmosphere.

distractors: Moving Mucus Matters for Lung Health
titles.why: The whole passage describes the lungs: where they are, what they do and which muscles drive breathing; mucus, the atmosphere and extinction are not its subject.

source.author: wikipedia

interactive.title: Can an Internet Program Help Mothers Lose Weight After Pregnancy?
interactive.text: Gaining weight in pregnancy is important for the health of the mother and child. However, after having a baby, if a mother keeps the extra weight she gained during pregnancy, this can be harmful to her long-term health. This study tested whether an Internet weight-loss program could help mothers to lose weight after having a baby. We worked with WIC, which is a program that gives low-income families food and support. Half of the women in the study received regular WIC and half received WIC plus an Internet weight-loss program. We found that the Internet program helped mothers lose five more pounds than regular WIC, and it also helped more mothers get back to the weight that they were before pregnancy. WIC serves half of all US mothers; the Internet weight-loss program in WIC could help many women get closer to the weight they were before pregnancy and avoid weight-related diseases later in life.

blanks.why: An adjective is needed after 'is', and 'important for the health' makes sense here.
'However' shows a contrast: gaining weight is good during pregnancy, but keeping it afterwards can be harmful.
The singular subject 'a mother' needs 'keeps', and a mother 'keeps' (does not lose) the extra weight.
'However' signals a problem, so keeping the weight 'can be harmful to her health'; after 'be' we need an adjective, and 'harm' is a noun or verb.
'Tested whether' introduces a yes/no question; 'weather' sounds the same but means rain and sun.
After 'to' a base verb is needed: 'lose weight'; 'loose' is an adjective and 'loss' is a noun.
'Which' adds information about WIC, a program (a thing), not a person.
The singular 'a program that' needs 'gives', and WIC gives families food and support.

distractors: Birth mothers who do not receive regular prenatal care are at higher risk of having a baby with low birth weight.
For example, folate is a B vitamin particularly important to fetal development and readily available in leafy green vegetables.
Researchers have investigated the relationship between premature labor and socioeconomic status, food insecurity, and stress.
missing.why: The next sentence compares the Internet program with 'regular WIC', so the missing sentence must explain that the women were split into these two groups.

highlights.question: How much more weight did mothers in the Internet program lose than mothers with regular WIC?
What illnesses could the program help women avoid, and when?

idea.answer: An Internet weight-loss program helped new mothers lose more weight than regular WIC alone.
distractors: Women should try not to gain any weight at all while they are pregnant.
Mothers who do not get regular prenatal care often have babies with low birth weight.
Most mothers in the study lost all of their pregnancy weight within one month.
idea.why: The study found that the Internet program helped mothers lose five more pounds than regular WIC.

titles.answer: Can an Internet Program Help Mothers Lose Weight After Pregnancy?
distractors: Care of Infants with Low Birth Weight
titles.why: The whole passage describes a study that tested whether an Internet program helps mothers lose weight after having a baby; the other titles are about pregnancy and babies.

source.title: Can an Internet Program Help Mothers Lose Weight After Pregnancy?
source.author: Adrian Mercado, Suzanne Phelan
