interactive.title: Rainforest
interactive.text: The canopy is like a huge green roof over the forest. The trees grow up thin and straight, like pillars seeking the sun. They do not put out branches until they are very tall. Then, they spread out like an umbrella in the sunlight. The trees are so close together that very little light penetrates through to the lower layers. Many kinds of monkeys, birds, and insects live in the layer. The animals that call this layer home often never touch the ground throughout their entire lives. They find everything they need existing within the canopy. Water can be accessed from the boles of trees, if not, the leaves and epiphytes that grow in the canopy can supply that need. The animals eat the leaves and fruit of the trees, insects, or other animals. The tall canopy trees must be able to reach the sunlight high in the air and still get nutrients from the thin soil on the forest floor. Their roots do not go deep into the soil because there is nothing there for the plants to reach.

blanks.why: The canopy is high 'over the forest', like a roof; a floor or basement is at the bottom.
'Not ... until' means the branches only come when the trees are very tall.
The plural 'they' needs the base verb, and branches 'spread out' like an open umbrella.
'So + adjective + that' shows a result: the trees are so close that little light gets through.
'Light' is uncountable, so we say 'very little light', not 'very few light'.
After 'Many' a plural noun is needed: 'many kinds of' means many types of.
The plural subject 'monkeys, birds, and insects' needs the verb 'live'.
'Call a place home' is a fixed phrase meaning to live there.

distractors: Here there is very little space between trees, resulting in thick layers of leaf covering that prevent much sunlight from reaching the forest floor.
Centered on the Congo River Basin, the rainforest is densest in the present-day central state of the Democratic Republic of Congo.
Elephants swim in rivers when they are hot.
missing.why: The animals never touch the ground, so they must find everything they need in the canopy; the next sentence then explains how they meet 'that need' for water.

highlights.question: What do the animals living in the canopy eat?
Why do the roots of the tall canopy trees stay close to the surface?

idea.answer: Many animals that live in the canopy never touch the ground in their whole lives.
distractors: Canopy trees have long roots that reach deep into rich soil.
So much sunlight reaches the forest floor that many plants grow there.
The thickest rainforest in Africa is found around the Congo River.
idea.why: The passage says the animals that call the canopy home often never touch the ground throughout their entire lives.

distractors: Geographic Diversity on the African Continent
titles.why: The passage describes the rainforest canopy, its tall trees and the animals living in it; roots are only mentioned at the end, and Africa and sanderlings are not discussed.

source.title: Rainforest
source.author: simple wiki
source.note: “Rainforest”, simple wiki (simple.wikipedia.org), CC BY-SA 3.0 and GFDL; via the CommonLit CLEAR corpus

interactive.title: How Olokwango Hill Lost Its Springs
interactive.text:
Olokwango hill stood smiling at the middle of Kwere Plains. From its side, came springs which joined downhill to form River Temu. Its waters were a gift to the sheep and goats of the area as well as the deer that dwelt in the plains.

Things were all well until Matata became headman. He ordered a path to be cleared from the top of the hill to the foot so that he could climb uphill easily and roll gently down to the foot. Olokwango hill was angry with the damage to his beard, but he was patient.

During the weekend, Matata's children and their friends would climb uphill to play. They would run all over the place, breaking twigs and branches, lighting fires for their games, which they would later leave burning.

Over time, Olokwango lost patience. The dimples became smaller and smaller as his face turned into ugly wrinkles. At last the springs were no more. The deer in the plains migrated because there was no more tall green grass to play in. The sheep and goats grew thinner and thinner. Everyone felt the sadness of Olokwango hill.

blanks.why: 'Which' introduces a clause about the springs, which are things, not people.
After 'to' a base verb is needed: the springs joined 'to form' (make) a river.
After 'a' a singular noun is needed; the water was a gift (something good) for the animals.
'All well until' means things were good up to the moment Matata became headman.
Something cleared from the top of a hill to the foot so he can climb is a path.
An adverb is needed to describe how he would climb: 'climb uphill easily'.
After 'was' an adjective is needed, and 'angry with the damage' fits the hill's feeling.
'But' shows contrast: the hill was angry, yet he stayed patient.

distractors: She had been sleeping outside for over a week.
If he couldn't find a wife, perhaps he could make one?
They were going home after spending the whole day in the fields.
missing.why: The next sentence says 'They would run all over the place', so the missing sentence must introduce the children who climbed up the hill to play.

highlights.question: Why did Matata want a path cleared from the top of the hill to the bottom?
Why did the deer leave the plains?

idea.answer: After people damaged the hill, its springs dried up and the animals of the plains suffered.
distractors: Matata planted new trees on the hill to make Olokwango happy again.
The children always put out their fires before they went home.
The sheep and goats grew fat because the river gave them plenty of water.
idea.why: The passage shows how the path and the children's fires damaged the hill until the springs dried up, the deer left and the sheep and goats grew thin.

titles.answer: How Olokwango Hill Lost Its Springs
distractors: Searching for the spirit of Spring
titles.why: The whole passage tells how Olokwango hill was damaged until its springs disappeared; nobody searches for spring, makes a wife or saves a dove.

source.title: The happy revival
source.author: Rebecca Njuguna
source.note: “The happy revival”, Rebecca Njuguna (africanstorybook.org), CC BY 4.0; via the CommonLit CLEAR corpus

interactive.title: The baboons that went this way and that
interactive.text: Other families noticed how well the hill family lived. "It is a good life up in the hills," said the husband. "You should come there too." Soon the other families left the flat land and went up to the hills. Each family found a cave to live in, and felt warm and secure. Soon the children became very quick at climbing rocks, and finding fruit in the trees. They could swing in the branches almost as well as any monkey. Slowly, things began to change. The children talked less, and grunted more. Then the adults noticed that their noses were getting bigger and that they were growing more hair. Every time they looked at one another they saw that their teeth were longer. They started to walk on four legs. They became a new creature that no-one had seen before in that place. This was the creature which people now call the baboon.

blanks.why: An adverb is needed to describe how they 'lived': 'how well', not 'how good'.
After a quotation, 'said the husband' tells us who spoke; 'told' and 'talked' are not used this way.
'Too' means 'also' at the end of a sentence; 'to' and 'two' only sound the same.
The story is in the past, like 'went', so 'left the flat land' is needed.
'Family' is singular, so only 'Each' fits; 'All', 'Both', 'Many' and 'Several' need plural nouns.
After 'felt' an adjective is needed, and 'warm and secure' describes life in the cave.
After 'became very' an adjective is needed: 'quick at climbing' means good and fast at it.
After 'could' a base verb is needed, and monkeys 'swing' in branches.

distractors: Eventually, curiosity got the better of the boys.
But there were several huge baboons in the troop.
When the tyrant jumped the others jumped, when he sat down the others sat down.
missing.why: The last sentence says 'This was the creature', so the missing sentence must first say that they became a new creature.

highlights.question: What did each family find after moving to the hills?
How did the children's way of speaking begin to change?

idea.answer: The families who moved to the hills slowly changed into the animal now called the baboon.
distractors: A cruel baboon leader made all the other baboons copy everything he did.
The families went back to the flat land because life in the caves was too hard.
The children taught the monkeys how to climb rocks and find fruit.
idea.why: The passage describes how the families' bodies and habits changed until they became the creature people now call the baboon.

titles.answer: The baboons that went this way and that
titles.why: The whole passage tells how the families who moved to the hills became baboons; it is not about a baboon leader, a monkey or a zebra.

source.author: Southern African Folktale

interactive.title: Queen of Soweto: The Story of Basetsana Kumalo
interactive.text:
When she was a child, Bassie was very shy. She liked to sing and dance in her room on her own. One day at school netball practice, the coach told two girls to pick teams. Bassie stood on the edge of the field hoping someone would say, "Come play with us!" But nobody wanted her on their team. Little did they know, Bassie would become one of the most popular girls in the country.

On weekends, she and her brother and sisters helped their teacher mom and bus driver dad to pay the bills. They made sandwiches to sell at local soccer matches. They tried to sell everything as fast as they could so they had time to play with the other children when the game was over.

By the time Bassie turned 16, she was a beautiful young woman. She was so beautiful that she won two beauty competitions in one year: Miss Soweto and Miss Black South Africa. But Bassie was not only beautiful on the outside. She was also beautiful on the inside. Even though she was a beauty queen, she still cared about the community where she grew up.

blanks.why: After 'was very' an adjective is needed, and 'shy' fits a girl who sang and danced alone.
'On her own' is a fixed phrase meaning alone.
'Told someone to do something' is the right pattern; 'said' and 'talked' cannot be followed by 'two girls to'.
'Stood ... hoping' describes what she was wishing while she stood there.
'But' shows contrast: she hoped to be picked, yet nobody wanted her.
'Their team' needs the possessive 'their'; 'there' and 'they' only sound similar.
After 'would' a base verb is needed: 'would become'.
'One of the most popular' is the superlative pattern; 'mostly' is an adverb and cannot come before 'popular' here.

distractors: The boys told her to go and play netball.
The coach was worried because his best player was sick and could not play.
We went home really tired, but the practice was good.
missing.why: The next sentence says they tried to 'sell everything' before 'the game was over', so the missing sentence must say what they sold and where.

highlights.question: Whom did Bassie and her brother and sisters help on weekends?
Which two beauty competitions did Bassie win in the same year?

idea.answer: Bassie was a shy child who grew up to become a beauty queen and still cared about her community.
distractors: Bassie was picked first for the netball team because everyone wanted to play with her.
Both of Bassie's parents worked as teachers at her school.
Bassie stopped caring about her community after she became a beauty queen.
idea.why: The passage says Bassie was very shy as a child, later won two beauty competitions, and still cared about the community where she grew up.

titles.answer: Queen of Soweto: The Story of Basetsana Kumalo
titles.why: The whole passage tells the life story of Basetsana (Bassie) Kumalo from shy child to beauty queen; soccer is only a small detail.

source.title: Queen of Soweto: The Story of Basetsana Kumalo
source.author: Jessica Taylor
source.note: “Queen of Soweto: The Story of Basetsana Kumalo”, Jessica Taylor (africanstorybook.org), CC BY 4.0; via the CommonLit CLEAR corpus

interactive.title: The Universe of the Very Small
interactive.text:
The foregoing discussion has likely impressed on you that the universe is extraordinarily large and extraordinarily empty. On average, it is 10,000 times more empty than our Galaxy. Yet, as we have seen, even the Galaxy is mostly empty space. The air we breathe has about 1019 atoms in each cubic centimeter—and we usually think of air as empty space. In the interstellar gas of the Galaxy, there is about one atom in every cubic centimeter. Intergalactic space is filled so sparsely that to find one atom, on average, we must search through a cubic meter of space. Most of the universe is fantastically empty; places that are dense, such as the human body, are tremendously rare.

Even our most familiar solids are mostly space. If we could take apart such a solid, piece by piece, we would eventually reach the tiny molecules from which it is formed. Molecules are the smallest particles into which any matter can be divided while still retaining its chemical properties. A molecule of water, for example, consists of two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom bonded together.

blanks.why: 'Impressed on you that ...' introduces the idea you have learned, so 'that' is needed.
'10,000 times more' compares amounts; after a number we need the plural 'times'.
A comparison with 'more empty' needs 'than'; 'then' is about time.
'We breathe' needs the verb; 'breath' is the noun.
'Think of X as Y' is a fixed pattern meaning to consider X to be Y.
'Every' goes with a singular noun ('cubic centimeter'); 'all', 'many', 'both' and 'few' need plurals.
An adverb is needed after 'filled so', and 'sparsely' (thinly) matches having to search a whole cubic meter to find one atom.
After 'must' a base verb is needed, and we 'search through' space to find an atom.

distractors: Moving around this proton is a single electron.
Helium, for example, is the second-most abundant element in the Sun.
Making an ion from an atom or molecule is called ionization.
missing.why: 'Such a solid' refers back to the familiar solids in the sentence before, and the 'molecules' it mentions are explained in the next sentence.

highlights.question: How much matter is there in the gas between the stars of our Galaxy?
What is a water molecule made of?

idea.answer: Most of the universe is almost completely empty, and dense places like the human body are very rare.
distractors: Solid objects are packed so tightly that they contain almost no empty space.
Our Galaxy is about 10,000 times emptier than the universe as a whole.
There are more atoms in each cubic centimeter of intergalactic space than in the air we breathe.
idea.why: The passage says most of the universe is fantastically empty and that dense places, such as the human body, are tremendously rare.

titles.answer: The Universe of the Very Small
titles.why: The passage moves from the emptiness of the universe down to the tiny molecules that matter is made of; atomic nuclei, ions and carbon bonds are not discussed.

source.title: The Universe of the Very Small
source.note: “The Universe of the Very Small”, Astronomy 2e, OpenStax (Rice University), CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

interactive.title: Modeling
interactive.text:
Many anthropologists create models to help others visualize and understand their research findings. Models help people understand the relationships between various points of data and can include qualitative elements as well. One very familiar model is a map. Maps are constructed from many thousands of data points projected onto a flat surface to help people understand distances and relationships. Maps are typically two-dimensional, but we are of course all familiar with the three-dimensional version of a world map known as a globe. Maps and globes are built on data points, but they also include qualitative information, such as the colors used to represent various features and the human-assigned names of various geographical features. Other familiar types of models include graphs, calendars, timelines, and charts. GPS is also a significant modeling tool today.

GPS, or the Global Position System, is increasingly used in archaeology. A model of a research site can be created using computer programs and a series of GPS coordinates. Any artifacts found or important features identified within the site can mapped to their exact locations within this model.

blanks.why: 'Their research findings' needs the possessive 'their' (the anthropologists' findings).
'Relationships between' things is the usual collocation.
After 'can' a base verb is needed: 'can include' means can contain.
An adjective is needed before 'model': a map is a very familiar (well-known) model.
'Are constructed from' is a passive verb meaning are built from.
An adjective is needed before 'surface', and maps are drawn on a flat (two-dimensional) surface.
'But' shows contrast between two-dimensional maps and the three-dimensional globe.
'Known as' is a fixed phrase meaning 'called'.

distractors: Features such as trails, roads, and house pits are documented and included in a full set of field notes.
A genetic map is an illustration that lists genes and their location on a chromosome.
Statistics created from quantitative data help researchers understand trends and changes over time.
missing.why: The last sentence refers to 'the site' and 'this model', so the missing sentence must explain how a model of a research site is made with GPS.

highlights.question: What kinds of qualitative information do maps and globes include?
What can researchers place at their exact locations in a GPS model of a site?

idea.answer: Anthropologists use models such as maps, globes and GPS to help people understand their research.
distractors: Maps are built only from numbers and contain no qualitative information.
Archaeologists have stopped using GPS because it cannot show exact locations.
Most anthropologists avoid models because they make research findings harder to understand.
idea.why: The passage explains that anthropologists create models, such as maps, globes and GPS models, to help others understand their findings.

distractors: Differences between Quantitative and Qualitative Information
titles.why: The whole passage is about the models anthropologists use, such as maps, globes and GPS models; it does not discuss dating, genomes or the difference between kinds of data.

interactive.title: Asthma in Middle Childhood
interactive.text:
Although middle childhood is generally a healthy period for many children, there are some common health issues that are often seen during middle childhood, such as asthma and diabetes.

Asthma is a life-long, chronic lung disease that causes inflammation in the airways, making it difficult to breathe. Asthma is a serious public health problem globally. It affects about 8 percent of children in the United States. Although there is no known single cause of asthma, a child is more likely to have asthma if other family members have asthma, if they have other allergic conditions, if they live in urban areas or areas with high air pollution, and if they have obesity. Avoiding common triggers of asthma, including air pollution and allergies, can reduce the symptoms of asthma such as shortness of breath and tightness in the chest. Although it can typically be medically managed, uncontrolled asthma is one of the leading causes of school absences among children and can also interfere with sleep and physical activity.

blanks.why: An adjective is needed before 'period': middle childhood is generally a healthy time.
'There are' introduces something that exists; 'their' and 'they' cannot start this clause.
'During' + a period of time ('middle childhood'); 'while' needs a clause with a verb.
'Such as' introduces examples: asthma and diabetes.
The singular 'a ... disease that' needs the verb 'causes'; 'because' and 'causal' are not verbs.
'Making it difficult to breathe' is the pattern 'make it + adjective + to'; inflamed airways make breathing hard.
An adjective is needed before 'public health problem': asthma is a serious problem.
'Affects' is the verb (has an effect on); 'effects' is usually a noun, and 'It' needs the -s form.

distractors: In the short term, poor nutrition is related to excess weight gain and constipation.
After we eat sugar, our bodies release a hormone called insulin, which helps muscle and fat cells to take up and store sugar.
As long as the fat tissue can store extra energy, everything is fine.
missing.why: The sentence before lists causes such as air pollution and allergies; the missing sentence says avoiding these triggers reduces symptoms, and the next sentence goes on to how asthma is managed.

highlights.question: Where in the body does asthma cause inflammation?
Apart from school attendance, what can poorly controlled asthma disrupt?

idea.answer: Asthma is a common lung disease in middle childhood, but it can usually be managed with medical care.
distractors: Asthma is caused by a single gene that children get from their parents.
Most children in middle childhood have diabetes because they eat too much sugar.
Children with asthma should stop all physical activity to avoid breathing problems.
idea.why: The passage says asthma is a common health issue in middle childhood and that it can typically be medically managed.

distractors: From Mice to Humans: The Study of Obesity
titles.why: The passage is mainly about asthma in middle childhood: its causes, its symptoms and its effects on school, sleep and activity; it does not discuss nutrition, mental health or obesity research.

interactive.title: Galileo and the Beginning of Modern Science
interactive.text:
Many of the modern scientific concepts of observation, experimentation, and the testing of hypotheses through careful quantitative measurements were pioneered by a man who lived nearly a century after Copernicus. Galileo Galilei, a contemporary of Shakespeare, was born in Pisa. Like Copernicus, he began training for a medical career, but he had little interest in the subject and later switched to mathematics. He held faculty positions at the University of Pisa and the University of Padua, and eventually became mathematician to the Grand Duke of Tuscany in Florence.

Galileo’s greatest contributions were in the field of mechanics, the study of motion and the actions of forces on bodies. It was familiar to all persons then, as it is to us now, that if something is at rest, it tends to remain at rest and requires some outside influence to start it in motion. Rest was thus generally regarded as the natural state of matter. Galileo showed, however, that rest is no more natural than motion.

blanks.why: An adjective is needed before 'measurements', and science needs careful (exact) measurements.
The plural subject 'Many of the ... concepts' needs the past plural 'were'.
'Who' is the subject of 'lived' and refers to a man, a person.
After 'a' a singular time noun is needed: 'nearly a century after' means almost 100 years later.
'Was born in' tells where a person's life began.
An adjective is needed before 'career': a medical career is a career as a doctor.
'Interest' is uncountable here, so 'little interest' (not much) is correct; 'few' and 'many' need plural nouns.
The past-tense story needs 'held'; to 'hold a position' means to have a job.

distractors: Although he did not invent the telescope, he used it when he looked into the night sky.
Scientists use the term velocity to describe the speed and direction of motion.
In Newton’s time, gravity was something associated with Earth alone.
missing.why: The missing sentence concludes that people saw rest as the natural state of matter, which the next sentence then contradicts with 'however'.

highlights.question: Where did Galileo hold faculty positions?
According to common belief, what does a resting object need in order to begin moving?

idea.answer: Galileo showed that being at rest is not more natural for objects than being in motion.
distractors: Galileo was the first person to invent the telescope.
Galileo trained as a doctor and worked in medicine for most of his life.
Galileo agreed with the common belief that rest is the natural state of matter.
idea.why: The last sentence says Galileo showed that rest is no more natural than motion.

titles.answer: Galileo and the Beginning of Modern Science
titles.why: The passage introduces Galileo's life and his new ideas about motion, which helped begin modern science; Copernicus, friction and Newton's gravity are not its subject.

source.title: Galileo and the Beginning of Modern Science

interactive.title: Shocking
interactive.text:
It was not so much how hard people found the challenge but how far they would go to avoid it that left researchers gobsmacked. The task? To sit in a chair and do nothing but think.

So unbearable did some find it that they took up the safe but alarming opportunity to give themselves mild electric shocks in an attempt to break the tedium.

Two-thirds of men pressed a button to deliver a painful jolt during a 15-minute spell of solitude.

Under the same conditions, a quarter of women pressed the shock button. The difference, scientists suspect, is that men tend to be more sensation-seeking than women.

The report from psychologists at Virginia and Harvard Universities is one of a surprising few to tackle the question of why most of us find it so hard to do nothing.

In more than 11 separate studies, the researchers showed that people hated being left to think, regardless of their age, education, income or the amount of time they spent using smartphones or social media.

blanks.why: 'How hard people found the challenge' means how difficult it was; 'hardly' means almost not.
After 'go to' a base verb is needed: 'how far they would go to avoid it'.
After 'To' a base verb is needed, and we 'sit in a chair'.
'Do nothing but think' means the only thing to do was think.
People gave themselves shocks 'to break the tedium', so sitting still felt unbearable (too hard to stand).
The subject is 'they', so the reflexive pronoun must be 'themselves'.
After 'to' a base verb is needed, and 'break the tedium' means end the boredom.
'During' + a period of time ('a 15-minute spell'); 'while' needs a clause with a verb.

distractors: They feel less responsible because of the presence of other bystanders.
The devices let the animals work together on simple tasks to earn rewards, such as a drink of water.
It also tries to find out how happy they feel about using them.
missing.why: The next sentence explains 'the difference' between men and women, so the missing sentence must give the result for women to compare with the two-thirds of men.

highlights.question: According to scientists, why might more men than women have pressed the button?
Which personal details made no difference to how much people disliked being left alone to think?

idea.answer: Many people dislike sitting alone with their thoughts so much that some would rather give themselves electric shocks.
distractors: Women were more likely than men to press the shock button.
People who use smartphones a lot found it much harder to sit and think than other people.
Most people enjoyed having fifteen quiet minutes to relax and think.
idea.why: The passage reports that people hated being left to think and that some gave themselves mild electric shocks to break the boredom.

distractors: The Bystander Effect and Diffusion of Responsibility
titles.why: 'Shocking' fits the whole passage, which reports a study where people gave themselves electric shocks rather than sit and think; the other titles are about other studies.

source.title: Shocking
source.note: “Shocking” (advanced version), OneStopEnglish corpus (Vajjala & Lučić, 2018), CC BY-SA 4.0

interactive.title: How to Tell a Spider-Man from a Spider-Woman
interactive.text: You probably know of many animals in which the males and females look very different. Male lions, for example, have beautiful manes, while lioness do not. In birds, males tend to be beautifully colored, while the females are not—just think of ducks, chicken, or peacocks. But do you know how to distinguish spider-men and -women? Usually, female spiders are bigger, but only if they are well-fed. Females can also be a different color than the males of their species, but this is not true for all species. You can use another really safe trick to identify a male spider. In front of their four walking legs, both spider males and females have another pair of appendages, the pedipalps. The pedipalps are used for many of the spider skills explained above, like feeding, sensing, catching prey, and mating. And exactly on the tip of these pedipalps only adult male spiders have a specialized organ, which looks like boxing gloves.

blanks.why: 'Many' needs a plural noun, and lions, birds and spiders are the animals the passage goes on to describe.
'For example' is a fixed phrase that introduces an example.
'Tend to be' means 'are usually', and the plural subject 'males' takes 'tend', not 'tends'.
The plural subject 'the females' needs 'are' ('the females are not beautifully colored').
'Know how to' + verb means to know the way to do something.
The sentence compares body size: a spider gets bigger only if it eats well.
'A different color' needs a singular noun and continues the idea of colorful males and plain females.
'This is not true for all species' means the statement does not apply to every species.

distractors: Stripes, spots, and speckles are more common than solid.
Males usually have wings, but females are most likely wingless.
Females are usually about 1-1/2 inches long including their leg span.
missing.why: It introduces 'the pedipalps', which the next sentence goes on to describe, as part of the 'safe trick' for spotting a male spider.

highlights.question: Under what condition are female spiders usually larger than the males?
What does the special organ of adult male spiders look like?

idea.answer: Adult male spiders can be recognized by a special organ at the tips of their pedipalps.
distractors: People who are afraid of spiders usually imagine them to be bigger than they really are.
Female spiders are always a different color from the males of their species.
Male spiders use their pedipalps only for walking, never for catching prey.
idea.why: The last sentence says only adult male spiders have a specialized organ on the tip of their pedipalps, which is the 'really safe trick'.

titles.answer: How to Tell a Spider-Man from a Spider-Woman
titles.why: The passage explains the differences between male and female spiders: size, colour and the pedipalps.

source.title: The Process of Becoming a “Spider-Man”
source.author: Felix Simon, Christian Quade & Natascha Turetzek

interactive.title: Stay safe at the beach!
interactive.text:
When going to the beach, find out which ones have lifeguards. Always try to visit beaches that have lifeguards watching the swimmers. The lifeguards on duty will put red and yellow flags on the beach to show you where it is safe to swim.

Many people find it hard to see a rip current in the sea. Rip currents are like fast-flowing rivers that can pull even strong swimmers away from the beach.

This is why it is better to swim between the lifeguard flags.

If you get pulled out by a rip current, try not to panic. Try to swim to the left or to the right of the current's flow. Don't try to fight the current or to swim against the current. That will make you tired and more scared.

To be safe when you visit the beach, you should always listen to the lifeguards. And make sure that you stay between the red and yellow flags on the beach. The flags show you where the currents are safe.

blanks.why: 'Find out which ones' asks you to choose among the beaches; 'which' is used for things.
After 'try to' we need a base verb, and people visit beaches.
Lifeguards put red and yellow flags on the beach; the passage later talks about swimming 'between the lifeguard flags'.
'Find it hard to' + verb means it is difficult to do; 'hardly' is an adverb and does not fit here.
Rivers flow, so 'fast-flowing rivers' is a natural comparison, and the plural matches 'currents'.
After 'can' we need a base verb, and a strong current can pull a swimmer away.
'This is why' introduces the result of the danger described before.
You swim between two flags; the passage later says 'stay between the red and yellow flags'.

distractors: Throw something they can hold on to and use to stay above the water.
If the person who needs help is too far away from you to reach with a stick, you can throw something that floats.
The camper vans bring windsurfers and kitesurfers who are attracted by strong winds in the area.
missing.why: 'That will make you tired' in the next sentence refers to fighting or swimming against the current.

highlights.question: According to the first paragraph, why do the lifeguards on duty put red and yellow flags on the beach?
In which direction should you swim to get out of a rip current?

idea.answer: Swimming between the lifeguards' red and yellow flags is the safest way to avoid rip currents.
distractors: If someone is in trouble in the water, you should jump in and pull them out.
Rip currents are easy to see because the water in them is a different color.
Strong swimmers do not need to worry about rip currents at the beach.
idea.why: The passage says it is better to swim between the lifeguard flags because the flags show where the currents are safe.

distractors: How to help someone in water
titles.why: The passage gives advice on staying safe while swimming at the beach: choose beaches with lifeguards, swim between the flags and know how to escape a rip current.

source.title: Stay safe at the beach!
source.author: By Sea Rescue and Sean Verster

interactive.title: Detecting Ghostlike Neutrinos: Tiny Messengers From the Universe
interactive.text:
Neutrinos are very light particles with no electric charge. They are emitted when unstable atomic nuclei decay. Such radioactive decay happens all around us. Minerals in rocks and even potassium in bananas decay to produce neutrinos. But far more neutrinos come from the nuclear reactions in the sun than from any other source.

No matter what their source, neutrinos are completely harmless because they do not stick together or interact with much of anything. They stream from the sun and outer space and pass right through ordinary matter—even our own bodies and Earth itself—without us ever knowing. In that way, they seem a bit like ghosts—there, and yet invisible. But because neutrinos carry information about what is happening inside the hearts of stars and galaxies, scientists want to know a lot more about them. Neutrinos may even help us understand what was going on when our universe first formed nearly 14 billion years ago!

blanks.why: An adjective is needed before 'particles', and 'very light' describes how little they weigh.
'When' tells us at what moment neutrinos are given off: when nuclei decay.
The plural subject 'nuclei' needs 'decay', and the next sentence repeats the idea with 'Such radioactive decay'.
'All around us' means everywhere near us.
After 'to' we need a base verb, and decay produces (makes) neutrinos.
'Far more ... than' compares the sun with all other sources.
'No matter what' is a fixed phrase meaning 'whatever'.
An adjective is needed after 'completely', and the reason given (they do not interact with anything) shows they cause no harm.

distractors: The process of radioactive decay involves the emission of particles such as electrons, or of radiation in the form of gamma rays.
Every atom has in its center a very small nucleus.
For any one radioactive nucleus, it is not possible to predict when the decay process will happen.
missing.why: It says neutrinos pass through everything without us knowing, which the next sentence compares to ghosts with 'In that way'.

highlights.question: Where do most neutrinos come from?
Why do scientists want to learn more about neutrinos?

idea.answer: Neutrinos pass through ordinary matter, including our bodies, without causing any harm.
distractors: Neutrinos have a strong electric charge, so scientists can see them easily.
Most of the neutrinos around us come from bananas and other foods.
An invisible kind of matter makes up about a quarter of the universe.
idea.why: The passage says neutrinos are completely harmless and pass right through our bodies and Earth without us knowing.

titles.answer: Detecting Ghostlike Neutrinos: Tiny Messengers From the Universe
titles.why: The whole passage is about neutrinos: where they come from, why they are like ghosts and why scientists want to study them.

source.title: Detecting Ghostlike Neutrinos: Tiny Messengers From the Universe
source.author: Milind Vaman Diwan & Karen McNulty Walsh

interactive.title: Socrates
interactive.text:
As Socrates did not write down any of his teachings, secondary sources provide the only information on his life and thought. The sometimes contradictory nature of these sources is known as the Socratic problem, or the Socratic question.

Plato and Xenophon's dialogues provide the main source of information on Socrates's life and thought. These writings are the Sokratikoi logoi, or Socratic dialogues, which consist of reports of conversations apparently involving Socrates.

As for discovering the real-life Socrates, the difficulty is that ancient sources are mostly philosophical or dramatic texts, apart from Xenophon. There are no straightforward histories, contemporary with Socrates, that dealt with his own time and place. A corollary of this is that sources that do mention Socrates do not necessarily claim to be historically accurate, and are often partisan. For instance, those who prosecuted and convicted Socrates have left no testament. Historians, therefore, face the challenge of reconciling the various evidence from the extant texts in order to attempt an accurate and consistent account of Socrates's life and work. The result of such an effort is not necessarily realistic, even if consistent.

blanks.why: After 'did not' we need a base verb, and 'write down his teachings' means put them on paper.
'Secondary sources' are writings by other people; the plural matches the verb 'provide'.
'Sources' is plural, so it needs 'these', which points back to the sources just mentioned.
'Is known as' gives the name of something, here 'the Socratic problem'.
'A source of information' is a common phrase, and a noun is needed after 'of'.
'Which' starts a clause about things (the dialogues); 'who' is only for people.
'As for' is a fixed phrase meaning 'when it comes to'.
A singular noun is needed after 'the' and before 'is'; the sentence explains what makes finding the real Socrates hard.

distractors: Many thought Socrates was one of the sophists.
If a historian is looking at Ancient Egypt, a statue of a pharaoh is a primary source for that time period, as are hieroglyphs that tell of the pharaoh’s reign.
Primary sources, when we have them, are considered more valuable than other sources because they are as close in time as we can get to the events being studied.
missing.why: 'Therefore' draws a conclusion from the problems with the sources, and 'such an effort' in the last sentence refers to this attempt to build an accurate account.

highlights.question: What two names are given to the sometimes contradictory nature of the sources about Socrates?
What kind of writing about Socrates's own time and place does not exist?

idea.answer: Because Socrates wrote nothing himself, we can learn about him only through other people's writings.
distractors: Socrates wrote many books about his life that historians still read today.
Primary sources are more useful than other sources because they come from the time being studied.
Historians agree that the ancient sources give an accurate picture of Socrates's life.
idea.why: The first sentence says Socrates did not write down his teachings, so secondary sources provide the only information on his life.

titles.why: Every sentence is about Socrates and the problem of learning about his life from other people's writings.

source.author: wikipedia

interactive.title: The boy and the jackal
interactive.text: One day Jackal felt sick. He tried drinking water, but that made his stomach swollen. He tried eating grass but still his stomach hurt. Jackal decided that only the medicine of man would help him so he dragged himself off to the clinic in the town. "Auwwwh" said the nurse when she saw the bedraggled jackal, "this place is for sick people, not animals. Go away!" Now Jackal was a clever animal, so sick as he was, he made a plan. He asked a boy called Ernst who was sitting outside the clinic, to help him by fetching the medicine from the nurse. "If you do this for me, I will give you a fat, fresh bird for you cooking pot, everyday." Ernst was hungry and anyway, he felt sorry for the sick jackal, with his drooping whiskers and his tail hanging like a rag, so he went in and got the medicine and gave it to the jackal. Jackal licked up all the medicine at once and immediately his ears stood up and his tail lifted.

blanks.why: The story is in the past tense, and 'felt sick' describes how Jackal's body felt.
'But' shows that drinking water did not help as he hoped.
The story is in the past, and a sick stomach hurts ('hurt' is also the past form).
A sick animal needs medicine, and a noun is needed after 'the'; he goes to a clinic to get it.
'So' shows the result: because only man's medicine could help, he went to the clinic.
The subject is 'he', so the reflexive pronoun is 'himself'.
A clinic is for sick people, and the contrast 'not animals' shows the missing word is about humans.
We say 'make a plan' (not 'do a plan'), and the story needs the past form 'made'.

distractors: He spotted a bunch of juicy ripe grapes hanging from a high branch.
He jumped up and went searching for food.
He went closer and closer to the rock.
missing.why: It explains Jackal's plan, and 'this' in the next sentence ('If you do this for me') refers to fetching the medicine.

highlights.question: Why did the nurse tell Jackal to go away?
How did Jackal's body change after he licked up the medicine?

idea.answer: After the nurse refused to help him, Jackal got a boy to fetch the medicine for him.
distractors: Jackal jumped as high as he could to reach a bunch of ripe grapes.
The nurse gave Jackal the medicine because she felt sorry for him.
Ernst refused to help Jackal because he was afraid of wild animals.
idea.why: The nurse sends Jackal away, so he asks Ernst to fetch the medicine, and Ernst brings it to him.

distractors: Hungry Jackal and the sour grapes
Sly Jackal tricks the silly Donkey
titles.why: The story is about Jackal and the boy, Ernst, who helps him get medicine from the clinic.

interactive.title: Super Mummy and Super Super!
interactive.text: We have fun with children who come to the shop with their parents. Sometimes, mother has to serve as referee as well as help customers. I think that she has superpowers! When we become too noisy, mother says, "Now sit quietly and watch TV." She always adds, "But only for 30 minutes, while we take a break!" If we don't have schoolwork, sometimes mother asks me or my older sister to help her. I am not always ready to help. But I do it because I know she works so hard. As we walk home from the shop with the sun setting, we talk about our day. We have to hurry to keep up with her, but we love walking and talking with mother. She makes sure that we do homework and have time to play. She makes sure that we eat vegetables and fruits, and drink water. When we are sick, she cares for us.

blanks.why: 'Have fun' is a fixed phrase meaning to enjoy yourself; 'funny' is an adjective.
'Who' starts a clause about people (the children) and is the subject of 'come'.
A possessive word is needed before 'parents', and 'children' is plural, so 'their'.
'As well as' is a fixed phrase meaning 'and also'.
In a shop, mother helps customers, the people who buy things.
We say 'watch TV', and after 'sit quietly and' we need another base verb.
'Take a break' means to stop working and rest for a short time.
'Ask someone to do something' is the right pattern, and 'mother' needs the -s form.

distractors: Mother Hen is happy with her lovely chicks.
She will take her chicks to the fair.
She was worried and was going to search for Baby Mosquito.
missing.why: 'But I do it' answers the sentence before: the child is not always ready to help, but helps because mother works so hard.

highlights.question: What does mother tell the children to do when they are too loud?
What do the children and mother talk about on their way home from the shop?

idea.answer: Even though mother works hard at the shop, she makes sure her children are well looked after.
distractors: Mother leaves the children at home alone when she goes to work at the shop.
The children are allowed to watch TV for as long as they like.
Mother takes her children to the fair every evening after the shop closes.
idea.why: The child says mother works so hard, yet she makes sure they do homework, eat well and are cared for when sick.

titles.why: The child describes mother as a 'super' mum who runs the shop and still looks after the children.

source.author: Mimi Werna

interactive.title: Protein Structure
interactive.text:
As discussed earlier, the shape of a protein is critical to its function. To understand how the protein gets its final shape or conformation, we need to understand the four levels of protein structure: primary, secondary, tertiary, and quaternary.

The unique sequence and number of amino acids in a polypeptide chain is its primary structure. The unique sequence for every protein is ultimately determined by the gene that encodes the protein. Any change in the gene sequence may lead to a different amino acid being added to the polypeptide chain, causing a change in protein structure and function. William Warrick Cardozo showed that sickle-cell anemia is caused by a change in protein strucure as a result of gene encoding, meaning that it is an inherited disorder. In sickle cell anemia, the hemoglobin β chain has a single amino acid substitution, causing a change in both the structure and function of the protein. What is most remarkable to consider is that a hemoglobin molecule is made up of two alpha chains and two beta chains that each consist of about 150 amino acids. The molecule, therefore, has about 600 amino acids.

blanks.why: A singular noun is needed before 'of a protein is', and the next sentence talks about the protein's 'final shape'.
'A protein' is a singular thing, so the possessive is 'its'.
'Understand how' asks about the way the protein gets its shape.
After 'a' we need a singular noun, and amino acids are joined in a 'polypeptide chain'.
'Every' is followed by a singular noun ('every protein'); the other words need a plural.
'Is determined by' is a passive verb meaning 'is decided by'; the gene decides the sequence.
After 'may' we need a base verb, and 'lead to' means 'cause' (we cannot say 'cause to' or 'bring to' here).
'Being added to the chain' is passive: the amino acid is put into the chain.

distractors: When protein is digested, it is broken down into amino acids.
For example, proteins can function as enzymes or hormones.
Translation requires the input of an mRNA template, ribosomes, tRNAs, and various enzymatic factors.
missing.why: It gives details of the sickle-cell anemia named just before, and it introduces hemoglobin, which the next sentence describes.

highlights.question: What are the four levels of protein structure?
What is a hemoglobin molecule made up of?

idea.answer: A change in a gene can change a protein's structure and, as a result, the way it works.
distractors: Every protein has the same shape, so its shape does not affect how it works.
Sickle-cell anemia is caught from other people and is not passed down in families.
A hemoglobin molecule contains only about 150 amino acids in total.
idea.why: The passage says any change in the gene sequence may change the amino acids and so cause a change in protein structure and function.

titles.why: The passage explains the levels of protein structure and how a change in a gene can change a protein's structure.

source.title: Protein Structure
source.note: “Protein Structure”, Concepts of Biology, OpenStax (Rice University), CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

interactive.title: Postindustrial Society
interactive.text:
Information societies, sometimes known as postindustrial or digital societies, are a recent development. Unlike industrial societies that are rooted in the production of material goods, information societies are based on the production of information and services.

Digital technology is the steam engine of information societies, and computer moguls such as Steve Jobs and Bill Gates are its John D. Rockefellers and Cornelius Vanderbilts. Since the economy of information societies is driven by knowledge and not material goods, power lies with those in charge of storing and distributing information. Members of a postindustrial society are likely to be employed as sellers of services—software programmers or business consultants, for example—instead of producers of goods. Social classes are divided by access to education, since without technical skills, people in an information society lack the means for success.

blanks.why: 'Sometimes known as' gives other names for information societies.
The subject 'Information societies' is plural, so it needs 'are'.
'Unlike' + noun shows a contrast between industrial and information societies; the other words need a full clause.
'Rooted in' means 'based on'; after 'are' we need the past participle.
'Material goods' are physical things that are made and sold.
'Are based on' is a fixed passive phrase meaning 'have as their main part'.
The steam engine powered industrial societies, so digital technology is compared to it; 'the' + singular noun matches 'is'.
'Such as' is a fixed phrase that introduces examples.

distractors: In 1782, James Watt and Matthew Boulton created a steam engine that could do the work of twelve horses by itself.
Gathering-hunting societies such as the Hadza are highly mobile and egalitarian.
Cities and craft specialization are developed from the surplus generated by intensive agriculture.
missing.why: It explains who has power in an economy driven by knowledge, and it leads into the next sentence about people who sell services instead of producing goods.

highlights.question: Unlike industrial societies, what are information societies based on?
What divides social classes in an information society?

idea.answer: In an information society, people without technical skills find it hard to succeed.
distractors: Information societies are based mainly on factories that produce material goods.
Most workers in a postindustrial society are employed as producers of goods.
Societies are classified by how many people live in their cities.
idea.why: The last sentence says that without technical skills, people in an information society lack the means for success.

titles.why: The whole passage describes postindustrial (information) societies: what they produce, who has power and how people work.

interactive.title: The Era of Decline
interactive.text: Beginning around 1800 BCE, the centuries of trade between the Indus valley and Mesopotamia came to an end. Over the next four centuries, the cities of the Indus River valley were slowly depopulated, and the civilization declined, likely in stages. Why and how this decline occurred remains unknown. One common view is that it was related to regional climate change. Around 2000 BCE, the floodplain of the Indus River shifted dramatically, creating dry river beds where cities had been and water once flowed. Changes in the pattern of seasonal wind and rainfall, known as the monsoon in South Asia, may have caused these environmental effects. Without a secure source of water for drinking and irrigation, the cities would have suffered declines in population. Another theory suggests that centuries of environmental degradation caused by urbanization and large population growth made the land unsuitable to human populations. Still other views point to the possibility of tectonic activity that changed the course of the rivers, or even epidemic disease that decimated the population.

blanks.why: 'Trade between X and Y' describes buying and selling from one place to another.
'Came to an end' is a fixed phrase meaning 'stopped'.
The plural subject 'the cities' needs 'were' in this past passive verb.
The sentence is in the past, and a civilization that loses its people declines (becomes weaker).
'Remains unknown' means 'is still not known'; a verb with the -s form is needed for the subject 'Why and how this decline occurred'.
'Was related to' means 'was connected with'.
An adverb is needed to describe how the floodplain 'shifted': very greatly.
'Where' refers to a place: the river beds were in the places where cities had been.

distractors: The farmers of the Indus valley cultivated wheat and barley as well as raised cattle and sheep, as did the farmers of Mesopotamia and western Asia.
Instead, a common culture grew that was defined by urban planning, complete with advanced drainage systems, orderly streets, and distinctive bricks made in ovens.
Although the writing has not yet been deciphered, the evidence suggests they belonged to the same language system.
missing.why: 'Another theory' adds a second explanation after the climate-change view, and the next sentence continues the list with 'Still other views'.

highlights.question: According to one common view, what was the decline connected to?
What would the cities have lacked that caused their populations to fall?

idea.answer: No one knows for sure why the Indus valley civilization declined, but there are several possible explanations.
distractors: The Indus valley cities grew much larger after their trade with Mesopotamia ended.
The Indus valley civilization ended suddenly because of one great flood.
Historians have proved that a change in the monsoon was the only cause of the decline.
idea.why: The passage says why and how the decline happened remains unknown, and then lists several possible explanations.

distractors: The Origins of the Indus Valley Civilization
Vedic India to the Fall of the Maurya Empire
titles.why: The whole passage is about the period when the Indus valley civilization declined and the possible reasons for it.

interactive.title: DNA Repair
interactive.text: DNA polymerase can make mistakes while adding nucleotides. It edits the DNA by proofreading every newly added base. Incorrect bases are removed and replaced by the correct base, and then polymerization continues. Most mistakes are corrected during replication, although when this does not happen, the mismatch repair mechanism is employed. Mismatch repair enzymes recognize the wrongly incorporated base and excise it from the DNA, replacing it with the correct base. In yet another type of repair, nucleotide excision repair, the DNA double strand is unwound and separated, the incorrect bases are removed along with a few bases on the 5' and 3' end, and these are replaced by copying the template with the help of DNA polymerase. Nucleotide excision repair is particularly important in correcting thymine dimers, which are primarily caused by ultraviolet light. In a thymine dimer, two thymine nucleotides adjacent to each other on one strand are covalently bonded to each other rather than their complementary bases. If the dimer is not removed and repaired it will lead to a mutation. Individuals with flaws in their nucleotide excision repair genes show extreme sensitivity to sunlight and develop skin cancers early in life.

blanks.why: We say 'make mistakes' (not 'do mistakes'), and after 'can' we need a base verb.
The singular subject 'It' needs 'edits', and editing means checking and correcting.
'And then' shows what happens next, after the wrong base is replaced.
'During' + noun ('during replication') means 'in the time of'.
The plural subject 'enzymes' needs 'recognize': the enzymes find the wrong base before removing it.
'Another type of' means 'another kind of', and 'another' needs a singular noun.
'Along with' is a fixed phrase meaning 'together with'.
'With the help of' is a fixed phrase meaning 'using' or 'helped by'.

distractors: The replication of DNA occurs during the synthesis phase, or S phase, of the cell cycle, before the cell enters mitosis or meiosis.
Each new double strand consists of one parental strand and one new daughter strand.
Sunscreen should be reapplied every 2 h or after swimming, sweating, bathing, or using a towel.
missing.why: It explains what a thymine dimer is, right after thymine dimers are first named and before 'the dimer' in the next sentence.

highlights.question: How does DNA polymerase check the DNA for errors?
What mainly causes thymine dimers?

idea.answer: Cells have several different ways to find and fix mistakes that are made when DNA is copied.
distractors: DNA polymerase never makes mistakes when it adds new nucleotides.
Thymine dimers are harmless and never lead to mutations.
Mismatch repair enzymes add extra bases to the DNA instead of removing wrong ones.
idea.why: The passage describes proofreading, mismatch repair and nucleotide excision repair, which are all ways of fixing DNA mistakes.

titles.why: The passage explains the different ways that mistakes in DNA are found and corrected, which is DNA repair.

source.title: DNA Repair
source.note: “DNA Repair”, Concepts of Biology, OpenStax (Rice University), CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

interactive.title: Clouds and Global Warming
interactive.text:
A new scientiﬁc study says that global warming might make temperatures rise more than people think. The scientist who led the research said that, if emissions of greenhouse gases are not reduced, the planet will be at least 4C warmer by 2100. This is twice the level the world’s governments consider to be dangerous. The research shows that fewer clouds form as the planet warms. This means that less sunlight reﬂects back into space and this makes temperatures even higher. The way clouds affect global warming has been the biggest mystery in the study of future climate change.

Professor Steven Sherwood, at the University of New South Wales in Australia, who led the research, said that their work was new in two ways. First, it found what controls the cloud changes and, second, it did not accept the lowest estimates of future global warming; it believed the higher, more damaging estimates.

blanks.why: 'A study says that' reports what the study found; 'study' is singular, so 'says'.
'More than' compares two amounts: the real rise and what people think.
'If' gives the condition: the planet gets warmer if emissions are not reduced.
'Are not reduced' is passive, so it needs the past participle; reducing emissions means making them smaller.
'At least' is a fixed phrase meaning 'not less than'.
An adjective is needed after 'consider to be', and a temperature rise can be dangerous.
'Fewer' needs a plural noun, and clouds form in the sky and reflect sunlight.
Temperatures become 'higher' (we do not say 'taller'); 'even' before it needs a comparative.

distractors: Many scientists say that in the next 100–200 years, temperatures might be up to 6 degrees Celsius higher than they were before the effects of global warming were discovered.
When people use fossil fuels like coal and oil, this adds carbon dioxide to the air.
Evaporation is when water changes from liquid to gas.
missing.why: It says the work was new in two ways, which the last sentence then lists with 'First' and 'second'.

highlights.question: How much warmer could the planet be by 2100 if greenhouse gas emissions are not cut?
Which estimates of future global warming did the research believe?

idea.answer: Because fewer clouds form as the Earth warms, global warming may be worse than many people expect.
distractors: More clouds form as the planet warms, and this helps to cool the Earth down.
The new study accepted the lowest estimates of future global warming.
The world's governments believe a rise of 4C would be completely safe.
idea.why: The passage says fewer clouds form as the planet warms, so less sunlight is reflected and temperatures may rise more than people think.

distractors: Removing Harmful Greenhouse Gases from the Air Using Energy from Plants
titles.why: The passage reports a study showing that fewer clouds form as the planet warms, which could make global warming worse.

source.title: Planet
source.note: “Planet” (elementary version), OneStopEnglish corpus (Vajjala & Lučić, 2018), CC BY-SA 4.0

interactive.title: Producers in an Ecosystem
interactive.text: From the largest animals to the tiniest, an ecosystem can be organized by energy into a pyramid called the energy pyramid. At the bottom of the pyramid are producers, which are organisms that make their own food, such as plants. Plants produce food by taking in carbon dioxide from the air and water from the soil. Plants use sunlight to create sugars from the carbon dioxide molecules and water molecules. The plant moves sugars through its body and assembles these sugars into long chains of molecules called polysaccharides. The polysaccharides may be used immediately, or stored for later use by the plant. A plant may store several million calories of energy in this manner, enough to live for several weeks or more without sun. Most of this energy is glucose, a sugar that animals also need to survive. The rest of the organisms in the pyramid rely on the energy that comes from producers.

blanks.why: An ecosystem can be organized (arranged) into a pyramid; the other verbs do not describe arranging living things by energy.
“At the bottom of the pyramid” names a position in the pyramid; the other nouns are not places.
“which are organisms…” adds information about “producers”; only “which” can start this clause.
“make their own food” is a fixed phrase: producers make food themselves.
Plants take in (absorb) carbon dioxide; “take in” is the phrasal verb that matches “from the air”.
Plants take water from the soil through their roots.
Plants use sunlight (light energy) to make sugars.

distractors: The energy then flows from the plants to the animals that eat them.
When animals eat plants, they only use a small amount of the energy that the plants have stored.
The rest of the energy is lost as heat.
missing.why: The sentence before introduces polysaccharides, and the next sentence says the plant stores energy “in this manner”, which refers to storing them for later use.

highlights.question: What do plants use to create energy?
How can a plant survive for weeks without sunlight?

idea.answer: Producers are at the bottom of the energy pyramid and are the source of food and energy for the other organisms in the ecosystem.
distractors: The energy pyramid is a model that shows how energy flows from the sun to plants to animals, with most of the energy being lost as heat at each level.
The energy pyramid is a graphical representation of how energy is passed along from one organism to another in an ecosystem.
Animals at the top of the pyramid make their own food from sunlight and water.
idea.why: The passage explains what producers are, how they make and store food, and that the rest of the pyramid depends on them.

titles.why: The whole passage is about producers: what they are, how they make and store energy, and why other organisms need them.
